en: In the treatise *Bauddhālaṃkāra*, the first part, the *Subodhālaṃkāra* composed by Saṃgharakṣita, [ends]. 1.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One— homage to that Blessed One, the Samyaksambuddha—
the face of the Lord of Sages, [beheld] by the beautiful lady born from the womb of Bhoja.
My speech is a refuge for living beings; let it also lead my own mind. || 1 ||
May the Goddess of Speech—the beautiful one born from the interior of the lotus-face of the Lord of Munis—be my refuge for all living beings and gladden my mind. (1)
There exist ancient ornaments that are honored by Rāma and esteemed by the wise;
nevertheless, they do not employ the pure Māgadhikā meter.
Although there are ancient ornaments such as those of Rāmaśarman and others that exist among the wise,
nevertheless, those who seek pure knowledge do not employ them.
Even so, I shall indeed satisfy these [people] who are devoid of ornament;
this exertion of mine is for their sake, according to what is appropriate. (3)
Even by this, those devoid of ornaments might perhaps be satisfied;
yet this exertion of mine is for the sake of an ornament suited to them. (3)
Wisdom, which is praised as the unique weapon, was not poured into them;
though their delusion has been destroyed, they do not understand anything at all.
Those whose wisdom has not been accumulated through familiarity with various treatises,
being struck down by delusion, do not understand anything at all.
But those who lack the desire to serve the feet of their teachers here,
and who instead smear themselves with the dust from their feet— they alone are truly wise renunciants.
For those who do not serve at the feet of their gurus here in this world—those whose feet are covered with the dust of such gurus are indeed truly discerning. (5)
When poets whose eyes and minds are fixed upon the drama of poetry compose anything whatsoever, it does not produce anything further that causes wonder.
It is not at all surprising that poets (the masters of poetry), whose eyes and minds are fixed upon poetry and drama, compose whatever they please.
That very same [speech], when it is produced with inspired eloquence, is a source of wonder;
by means of it, even those who are untrained therein satisfy the wise. (7)
Those very [conceptions] are what appear to them; for that is indeed bondage accompanied by wonder, wherein even the learned find satisfaction, though they pay no heed to it. (7)
And what is called *bandha* (bond) consists of words joined together and free from defects;
it is of three kinds according to the distinction between the *padya*, *aja*, and *vimiśra* types. (8)
Furthermore, "bandha" (composition) refers to the word and its meaning joined together and free from defects;
it becomes threefold through the distinction between verse, prose, and their mixture. (8)
Furthermore, it is analyzed in two ways: with connection (*nibandha*) and without connection (*anibandha*); the ornaments of the stringing together [of words] are to be understood as the weaving. (9)
Furthermore, it is analyzed as being twofold: composed and uncomposed;
for that composition becomes most worthy of praise when adorned with poetic ornaments. (9)
Your lotus-face is irreproachable and your speech is irreproachable;
they shine beautifully when adorned—how much more so when unadorned! 10.
Your lotus-face is faultless and your speech is faultless;
indeed, they shine when adorned—how much more so when unadorned! 10.
Without the instruction of a teacher, a fool desires to cross over; he indeed incurs sin.
How could a wise person, O friend, fall into a state of ridicule? 11.
If a fool desires to adorn himself without the instruction of a guru,
how could he avoid becoming an object of ridicule for the wise?
Even the "fragrance" (gandha) that illuminates the ornaments of the poets' speech attains the status of being their very word, through the metaphorical application of that [word's] meaning. (12)
Even a literary work that illuminates the ornaments of a poet’s speech attains the status of being the "meaning" [of the word *kāvya*] through metaphorical usage of the term. (12)

Therein, ornaments are of two kinds according to the distinction between word and meaning; that which consists of the connection of words and meanings is called a string (āvalī), and when that is adorned, it is [an ornament]. 13.
For ornaments are of two kinds there, distinguished by word and meaning; indeed,
that series [of works] named *Śabdārthabandha* should be composed,
endowed with poetic qualities (*guṇas*) and ornaments (*alaṃkāras*), yet free from the thorns of defects (*doṣas*).
Such a person is not praised by the wise, just like that kind of maiden. || 14 ||

Even if it is endowed with poetic excellences (*guṇa*) and ornaments (*alaṃkāra*), if it is marked by even a trace of defects, it is not praised by the learned; it is like such a maiden [who, though possessed of virtues, is blemished]. (14)
Therefore, by great effort, it is better to strive for the removal of faults;
for if one were entirely free from faults, would one not surely possess all virtues? || 15 ||
Therefore, one should accomplish it with great enthusiasm, free from the hope for faults;
for if this [practice] is entirely free from defects, would it not indeed possess all virtues? (15)
Though devoid of ornaments, she is captivating when endowed with virtues;
she is faultless, being free from defects and possessed of qualities, like the moon. (16)
Though devoid of ornaments, she is captivating because she is endowed with virtues;
she is faultless, being free from defects like a bride possessed of excellent qualities. 16.
Various defects are considered to exist in words, sentences, and their meanings; I shall now explain their definitions along with examples. (17)
Regarding the various defects considered to exist in words, sentences, and their meanings, I shall now state their definitions along with illustrative examples. (17)
Contradictory, having another meaning, having a different meaning, defiled, and opposed;
that which is to be inferred, dependent on qualification, inferior in meaning, and meaningless. (18)

Faults of words, the unity of meaning in sentences, the use of established stylistic conventions, as well as being unconfused, intelligible, possessing restraint, and free from loss of sequence— [these are the qualities]. (19)
Excessive, deficient, disconnected, and likewise harsh; || 20 ||
Contradictory, with a different meaning, redundant, and afflicted;
likewise, contradictory, dependent on a qualification, deficient in meaning, and meaningless—these are [the faults]. (18)
The defects of words and sentences are: having a single meaning, broken style, as well as being disordered, vulgar, lacking pauses, and deviating from the proper sequence. (19)

Excessive expression, lack of meaning, lack of connection, harshness, immaturity, lack of propriety, broken style, doubtfulness, obscurity, and faulty ornamentation— these are the defects dependent upon the meaning of the sentence. (21)
Inappropriateness, lack of propriety, violation of style, ambiguity, vulgarity, and faulty ornamentation— these are indeed the defects that emerge from the meaning of the sentence. (21)
That is indeed "contradictory by another meaning" (viruddhatthantara) when its other meaning contradicts what is intended, as in: "The poison-cloud brings happiness to the people. (22)

That indeed is the "contradictory other-meaning" (viruddhārthāntara) in which another meaning, though arrived at [by implication], is contradicted; for example: "The cloud, though poisonous, would gladden the people."
That by which the qualificand (visesya) is further qualified is called an adhyārtha;
for example: "This firefly shines, illuminating everything without exception. || 23 ||
That by which the object of qualification (*viśeṣya*) is made excessive is called *adhyartha*, as for example:
"This glow-worm shines, having illuminated all the quarters. (23)
The comprehension of whose purpose is painful due to the differentiation of nature and so forth—that is defiled;
just as this beloved woman is embraced by her [in that state]. (24)
That in which the comprehension of the meaning is difficult due to the analysis of its nature and so forth is "afflicted" (*kliṣṭa*)—
for example: "By her, this beloved is embraced."
Whatever phrase is defiled, possesses a weak expression, or consists of *yamaka* (chiming) and the like—that too is included within the faults of defiled phrases. (25)
For that which consists of obscure words, a weak meaning, or such things as *yamaka* (rhyme/pun), is included within the fault of "obscure words" itself. (25)
That which is composed of well-falling syllables, possesses smooth transitions between words, and is endowed with the quality of clarity—such is considered *yamaka*. (26)
Yamaka (chiasmus) is that which arises from two or more syllables, being either non-separate (avyapeta) or separate (vyapeta);
it has as its domain the beginning, middle, and end of metrical feet. 27.

That *yamaka* which arises from one or more repeated syllables, whether contiguous (*avyapeta*) or non-contiguous (*vyapeta*), occurs at the beginning, middle, or end of metrical quarters (*pāda*). (27)
All people, whether virtuous or not, are distinguished by their qualities; yet they do not attain true seclusion while in the company of those who lack seclusion.
By virtue of their own discernment, all noble people—even those who possess discernment—fail to attain that discernment in the presence of ignoble people who lack it. || 28 ||
If all wholesome and unwholesome states—whether powerful or weak—had not yet gone [to their result], then there would have been no such thing as the occurrence of pleasure and pain. (29)

All [karmas], whether wholesome or unwholesome, powerful or powerless, or even those that have not yet arisen, remain until they have reached their completion as bestowers of pleasure and pain. || 29 ||
With the utmost reverence, may I offer repeated salutations to the Triple Gem, which is the worthy vessel for all homage—both that performed by me and that which remains to be performed. (30)
With attentiveness (mindfulness), I pay homage to the Three Jewels—
the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
May she, who has been respectfully honored, destroy [this] respectful salutation (or pain). 30.
The forest-dweller makes every lotus beautiful;
the Sugata, who brings benefit to all, has gone to the world to bring it together.
The lotus is capable of adorning the water;
[he is] the giver of water (the cloud).
The forest-dweller (the cloud) is capable of adorning the sky;
the Sugata (possessing an excellent gait).
That Sugata (Buddha),
establishing the world in harmony, is capable of bringing about its welfare.
This illustration of the uninterrupted *yamaka* has been shown;
by this method, other *yamakas* as well are to be understood.
This mere fraction of the uninterrupted *yamaka* has been demonstrated; other *yamakas* as well are to be understood by this same method. (32)
For them, there are exceedingly many sources of discord and division;
among these, some are easy to accomplish while others are extremely difficult. (33)
There are an extremely great number of divisions, arising from their various combinations;
among these, some are easy to perform while others are exceedingly difficult.
"Because those *yamakas* and the riddles are not exclusively sweet, I have overlooked them all, fearing they might cause weariness to my students. (34)
"Pairs of verses (yamaka) and riddles (prahelikā) are not exclusively sweet;
therefore, I have disregarded all such figures here out of fear of causing distress to my students."
Whatever contradicts place, time, art, the world, logic, or scripture—this section on contradictory statements is presented here by way of illustration. (35)
Whatever contradicts place, time, measure, the world, logic, or scripture is known as the "contradictory word" (*virodhin-pada*); this shall be made clear through examples. (35)
Whatever is to be said regarding the past is called "to be understood" (neyya), just as all directions appear white at night. (36)
When something not previously established is brought forward, they say it must be inferred;
for example: "All directions appear white at night. (36)
The wise everywhere hold such a person in high esteem; for it is rare to find one who can transcend the power of sound and its influence. 37.
Those who know everything everywhere do not highly esteem such a thing;
for the comprehension of the power of words is difficult to attain and transcends [ordinary] limits. || 37 ||
That which, having reached a qualifier, requires a further qualification may be a sevenfold [cognition], as when one sees even more with the eye. (38)
That [cognition] which depends upon a qualifier becomes meaningful only after it has reached that qualifier, just as one sees him again with the eye. (38)
Just as the sun rises, having eclipsed the light of the firefly and rendered it inferior, so too one should distinguish oneself from that which is inferior and thus become superior. (39)
That which is to be qualified by something inferior is called *hīnārtha* (having the sense of inferiority), as for example:
"The sun rises, having rendered the glowworm lusterless. (39)
Whatever is considered meaningless merely for the purpose of filling a metrical foot, such as:
"I pay homage even to the lotus-like feet of the Buddha. (40)
That which serves merely to fill out the meter and is devoid of meaning is considered *anartha* (useless);
for example: "I salute the lotus-feet of the Buddha, and also... (40).
That which is expressed both by its sound and by its meaning, yet where even more is said, is "single-meaning" (ekattha); for example: "This cloud shines, this cloud rains. (41)
That which is stated both in terms of its form and its meaning, yet is expressed again, is considered to have the same meaning; for example, "vārida" (giver of water) and "vārida" (cloud). (41)
"Remaining here, he has seen the seeds of the *kurava* tree that have fallen;
this Great Sage, with a serene countenance, inspires confidence in the great multitude. (42)
Abandoning here the sprouts and seeds of views at the sacred ford of birth,
the Great Sage, the Lord who is serene, brings great people to a state of grace.
Just as there might be a lapse in an undertaking begun or a failure in decorum, so too—oh, how wonderful—is your wisdom, your virtue, and your very nature! (43)
Just as there might be a break in the sequence of what has begun, or a fracture in the structure—so too, O wonder, is your wisdom one thing, your virtue another, and your nature yet another! 43.
Where confusion arises from the improper placement of words, that should be understood as "confused" (vyākīrṇa); an example of this is as follows.
That in which confusion arises due to the improper placement of words should be known as "disordered" (vyākīrṇa); an example of it is as follows. || 44 ||
This person, rejoicing and constantly recollecting the Sugata, bows to the One of Many Virtues for the sake of the welfare even of the wicked. (45)
Constantly recollecting the Sugata, this person bows with great devotion even to the wicked, always joyfully remembering what is beneficial. (45)
This is considered an example of what is understood through words that are distinct [from their literal meaning], as follows:
"O maiden, why is it that you do not desire me, who desire you? (46)
That which is devoid of distinguished expression is considered vulgar, as for example:
"O maiden, why is it that you do not desire me, who desires you? (46)
Something might become difficult to believe due to the connection of words;
even that is accepted as intelligible, just as in the case of "the beloved of Yābhavat. (47)

If, due to the joining of words (*pada-sandhāna*), something becomes somewhat difficult to understand, that too is considered acceptable provided it is not vulgar, as in the example: "O you whose beloved is Yābhavatī. (47)

In the passages already mentioned, the pause (yati) occurs at the division of words as indicated; however, that which is stated to be deficient in *tāya* (the number of syllables) is what is called "deficient in pause" (*yatihīna*). || 48 ||
In metrical compositions (*vṛtta*), the pause (*yati*) occurs at the places indicated;
that which is devoid of such [a pause] is called "lacking *yati*," and furthermore— || 48 ||

The *yati* occurs everywhere at the end of a foot, and especially after half [of a verse]; it may also occur within a word consisting of multiple syllables, both before and after [the break], and in some cases even in the middle of a word. (49)

The *yati* (caesura) occurs everywhere at the end of a quarter-verse, and especially at the end of a half-verse; furthermore, in some cases, it may occur within a word even when multiple syllables precede and follow it. (49)
In this regard, the examples and counter-examples are as follows:—
there, the examples and counter-examples are as follows:—
[I bow] with my head to that Tathāgata, who has the color of gold.
He seems to sprinkle all directions with streams of golden liquid. || 50 ||
I bow my head to that Tathāgata of golden hue, who seems to drench all the directions with streams of liquid gold. (50)

In the case of *sarosandhi* (vowel-sandhi), when there is elision of a case-ending (*vibhatti*) due to the dropping of a letter, there occurs a change of state (*aññathātva*); in that instance, the substitution of *y* and so forth may appear as if it were subsequent (*parādiva*). (51)

Just as in the case of the prior limit (*pūrvāntavat*), so too in certain instances within vowel sandhi (*svarasandhi*), the *yaṇ*-substitute should be regarded as the beginning of the subsequent element (*parādivat*) when considering the pause (*yati*). // 51 //

The endings of words beginning with *ca* and others are always dependent on the preceding word; however, when connected to *pāda* and so forth, they are always dependent on the following word as if it were the first member of a compound. (52)

The particles beginning with *ca* are always dependent on the preceding word, as if they were the final part of that word; while the particles beginning with *pra* are eternally connected with what follows, as if they were the initial part of that subsequent element. (52)
Examples for all cases are as follows:— I bow my head to that Tathāgata who has transcended all comparisons;
for no comparison is appropriate for him who has reached the summit of the world. (53)
Examples of [this] are as follows:—I bow my head to that Tathāgata who has transcended all comparison;
for one who has attained the pinnacle of the world, no comparison is indeed appropriate. (53)
I always pay homage to that Lord of Sages, whose infinite and supreme wisdom and loving-kindness manifest boundlessly. (54)
I always pay homage to that Lord of Munis, possessed of infinite and supreme intelligence, whose wisdom and loving-kindness expand boundlessly. (54)
Examples of *cādi-pādi* (conjunctions and particles) are as follows:
"I bow to that supreme Victor, the abode of excellent qualities, wherein Great Loving-kindness and Great Wisdom reach their highest manifestation. (55)

And as for counter-examples among the *ca*-class and *prādi*-class [particles], they are as follows: "I bow to that Jina, the most excellent one, the abode of supreme qualities, in whom great loving-kindness and great wisdom are the highest manifestations. (55)
Just as this [verse] deviates from the sequence of words and thus departs from the proper order—such as "Give me a beautiful field, or a village, or a country"—[so too is the following]. 56.
Just as this [world] is liberated from the sequence of categories (padārtha) and fallen from its order, so grant me a beautiful field, or a village, or a region. 56.
Just as the opinion that transcends worldly meaning is called "excessive" (ativutta), so too:
"The space is too cramped for the swelling of her breasts. (57)
Just as the opinion that space is exceedingly vast is considered to transcend the meaning of worldly experience, so too [is it said]: "Space is too narrow for the expansion of her breasts. (57)
Just as the son of a cowherd, though possessing the status of being part of a herd, is nevertheless distinct from that herd, so too does the ox eat grass and drink muddy water. 58.
That which is devoid of the meaning of the aggregate is "devoid of meaning" (apetārthaka); for example:
"The cow's son, the bull, ate the grass and drank the water. (58)
Where there is harshness in the binding, that is called "harsh binding"; just as seeds that are rough, unbroken, and fully decayed, when sown in a field, do not bear fruit at all. (59)
Where there is harshness in the composition, that is "harsh in its binding" (*bandhaparuṣa*), as for example:
"All the wicked have been utterly destroyed; sown in the field, they bear fruit in abundance. (59)
Now I shall demonstrate an illustration of these [types of meaning], such as the "to-be-led" (neyya), according to their characteristics and their respective applications. (60)
This is not a definition of *apakrama* and the others based on their literal meaning;
rather, I shall now demonstrate examples of these. (60)

The sequence therein is as follows:—The cultivation of meditation, generosity, and virtue, when perfectly accomplished here, are the means for attaining wealth, the celestial realms, and Nirvāṇa; of this there is no doubt. (61)
In that regard, the refutation is as follows:
"The practices of meditation, generosity, and ethical discipline, when correctly accomplished here,
are undoubtedly the means for attaining worldly enjoyments, the higher realms, and nirvāṇa."
An example of that which lacks propriety (*aucitya*):
"I am the most worthy of worship in the world, alone and without rival; for all virtues have arisen together within me alone. (62)
An example of what lacks propriety (*aucitya*) is as follows:
"I alone am perpetually the most worthy of worship in the world;
for all virtues are concentrated in me alone. (62)
And as it is said:
"When asked, how indeed could I not give even my life?
Nevertheless, my heart is pained by the thought of giving away my son. (63)
And as it is said:
"When entreated, how indeed could I not give even my life?
Nevertheless, at the thought of giving away my son, my heart trembles."
An example of a broken rule (bhaggarīti):
"Trust in women, in the wicked, in poison, in a thorn-bush, in disease, and in the royal court is not appropriate. (64)
An example of a broken rule (*bhagnarīti*):—
Trust is not to be placed in women, in wicked people,
in a horned animal, or in a river.
In illness and even in the royal court. || 64 ||
An example of that which involves doubt (*sasamsaya*):
The people, their eyes restless with the pleasure of beholding the moonlight of the Lord of Sages, were not satisfied, like a traveler on a path who has not yet reached his destination. (65)
An example of that which involves doubt:
With eyes eager for the pleasure of gazing upon the moon of the Lord of Sages, the people, though having already entered the path, were delighted by the sight of the cowherd boy. (65)

Just as the meaning of the statement "This man is vigorous; he will slay his enemy, do not be confident" is considered difficult to trust, so too is that which is to be understood [through inference]. (66)
That which causes a misconception due to the meaning of the sentence is considered *grāmya* (vulgar), as for example:
"This man, full of vigor, having slain the enemy, rested. (66)
That which is the defilement of ornaments is called "defective ornamentation" (duṭṭhālaṅkārananta).
Its definition will be made manifest under the section on "ornamentation" (alaṅkāra-niddesa). || 67 ||
But this is merely a perceived ornament where there is actually a flaw in an ornament;
its true nature will become manifest in the exposition of ornaments.
In this matter, I have here presented this preeminent classification of faults in brief;
for this alone is sufficient to instruct the poet, though there are others that would cause further weariness. (68)
This preeminent classification of defects has been made by me here according to a concise method;
it may be sufficient to instruct poets, even if it should prove excessively tedious. (68)
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Comprehension of Faults," in the *Subodhālaṅkāra* composed by the Great Master Saṅgharakkhita.
Thus [ends] the *Subodhālaṅkāra* composed by the Great Master Saṅgharakkhita.
The first chapter, titled "Understanding the Faults. Chapter Two:
An Exposition on Understanding the Avoidance of Faults.
Sometimes, even this entire collection of faults, when opposed by skill, transcends the number of defects and plunges into the path of virtues. (69)
Sometimes, through the skill of the poet, even this entire contradiction, transcending the number of faults, plunges into the path of poetic excellence. (69)
Now, the understanding of how to avoid the faults so that there may be no contradiction with what was stated by him is being set forth. (70)
Therefore, so that there may be no contradiction among those [statements] that appear contradictory,
the understanding of how to avoid such faults is now set forth.
In that regard, the resolution of the contradiction within the internal [context] is as follows:
"The sight of the rice-fields of the Sālins is a joy;
how then can this cloud, which brings destruction, be a joy to people? (71)

Among these, the avoidance of a contradictory secondary meaning (*viruddhārthāntara*) is as follows: "Finding joy from the sight of rice that is naturally ripe, how indeed could this cloud not bring happiness to the people? (71)
And as it is said:
"Though you are Vināyaka, you are also a Nāga; though you are Gotama, you are also Mahāmati; though you are Paṇita, you are also Rasāpeta."
O Master, my mind has gone to you. || 72 ||
And as it is said:

"Though you are Vināyaka, you are also a Nāga; though you are Gautama, you possess great intelligence; though you are Praṇīta, you are devoid of passion—O Lord, my devotion toward You is manifold. (72)
Regarding the internal meaning:
How can a wicked person, lacking such qualities, please the world? Even if he were illuminated like the sun, what would he be other than something to be devoured? (73)
An example of *adhyartha* (exaggeration): "How can a wicked person please the world in the absence of such qualities?
Could a mere firefly truly illuminate all the directions? (73)
Mounted upon a riddle, neither wicked nor defiled, who indeed does she embrace—she who is embraced by the bliss of love? (74)
In a riddle, the presence of obscurity is not a fault;
for who indeed would embrace that which is already embraced by the happiness of a beloved? || 74 ||
One should not employ a defiled word when a Yamaka is desired;
therefore, let everyone understand Yamakas to be exactly as we have [defined them]. (75)
If a defiled word is not employed where it is desired in a *yamaka*, then all other *yamakas* will be as if made of straw. (75)
An example of non-contradiction (*avirodhin*):
"By the power of the Bodhisattva, even on dry land we were called 'water';
as if dispelling for a very long time the distress of dwelling there in that water. (76)
Examples of contradictions with local custom (deśavirodhin):
By the power of the Bodhisattva, lotuses grew even on dry land;
and they seemed to dispel the long-standing misery of dwelling in that water. (76)
An example of contradiction with respect to time (*kālavirodhin*):
"Though the sage is of great majesty and his power is hidden, a gentle breeze blows through all seasons, shaking the flowers all at once. (77)
An example of [the fault] of contradiction with time (*kālavirodhin*):
"Though the sage was of great majesty, the wind was gentle;
for this [wind], blowing equally, brought all seasons' flowers at once. (77)

Examples of those that contradict the artistic convention (*kalāvirodhin*): "The mind of Pañcaśikha was submerged in the virtues of the Buddha; that discord of the lute strings did not please the audience. (78)
Examples of those incompatible with the occasion (kalāvirodhin) are as follows:
"Even though the mind of Pañcaśikha was immersed in the virtues of the Buddha, the discordance of the lute's notes did not please the Lotus-born One. (78)
An example of that which contradicts worldly convention: "He would consider the entire universe to be cooler than sandalwood paste, for the heart of a Bodhisattva is filled with glowing embers. (79)
An example of what contradicts worldly experience is as follows:
"The multitude of mountains, which is cooler even than sandalwood, [seemed] to him whose heart was intent on awakening to be filled with glowing embers. (79)
An example of contradiction between two meanings (*ññaya-virodhin*) is as follows: "Though you have abandoned existence, you are one who has attained existence;
homage to you, O bull among sages, whose essence consists of inconceivable virtues. (80)
Examples of those contrary to logic (nyāyavirodhin):— "Though you have transcended existence, you are indeed one who has entered into existence;
salutations to you, O bull among sages, whose essence consists of inconceivable qualities. (80)

Examples of those contradicting the scriptures (āgama): A monk who does not converse with anyone, yet makes vocal intimations, would incur an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) through intentional lying. (81)
Examples of those [actions] that contradict scripture:
"A monk who is eloquent does not speak with anyone at all, even when requested;
through such deliberate lying, he incurs the fault of an offense. (81)
Regarding one who is to be guided (*neyya*): Just as when the deceptive coating of a mirage is illuminated by light, all these white directions shine forth intensely. (82)
An example of that which is to be interpreted (*neyārtha*) is as follows:
"Because the rays of the sun have been made radiant by the application of sandalwood paste, all these directions shine intensely white. (82)
Or for example:
"The amorous play of women, which delights the mind, was not approved by the Jina; it is a fire in the heart of Māra. (83)
Or as it is said:
"The amorous dalliance of Māra’s maidens, which delights the mind, was not permitted by the Jina; it was a forest fire for the heart of Māra. (83)
An example of [the compound] requiring an adjective (*visesanāpekkha*):
"Even though he has committed no offense, this person looks upon his enemy with eyes that have become crimson with anger. (84)
An example of that which requires a qualification: "And this person looks again upon the enemy host, whose offenses have been removed, with eyes that have become crimson with anger. (84)
Regarding the inferior purpose:
"The wise man should destroy the power of even small evils;
for even the sun, when its light is extinguished, becomes like a glowworm devoid of radiance. (85)
An example of a base meaning: "A wise person should destroy the power of even small evils;
for even a glowworm, once its light is extinguished, becomes like the sun. (85)
Regarding what is useless—for example:
one should not employ a word anywhere merely for the sake of filling out the meter, such as:
"I pay homage to the excellent lotus-foot of the Lord of Sages. (86)
An example of that which is meaningless:
"One should not, under any circumstances, employ a word merely for the sake of filling out the meter.
For instance: "I bow to the excellent lotus-feet of the Lord of Munis. (86)
If such a distinction as fear, anger, praise, and so forth is intended to be expressed, no fault is committed therein by treating them as one. (87)
If one desires to speak with such distinctions as fear, anger, or praise, there is no fault therein; for in that case, the single intended meaning has not been established. (87)
For example:
"A snake! A snake! This one! Come now, turn back from here, sir! If you have any desire to live, why do you approach him? (88)
For example:
"Serpent! Serpent! Hey there! Turn back from here; if you desire to live, why do you approach him? (88)

An example of the *bhaggarīti* (the style of broken or interrupted rhythm): "Whatever excellence of form there may be, whatever charm of radiance, and whatever pre-eminence of grace—oh, the great arising of the Buddha! (89)
An example of *bhagnaprakrama* (broken sequence) is as follows:
"Whatever excellence of form there is, whatever indescribable loveliness, whatever extraordinary grace—oh, the great awakening is attained! (89)
The masters of poetry praise a composition that causes no confusion, is free from redundancy, is captivating, and has a smooth progression of its metrical feet. (90)
The masters of poetry praise that which causes no confusion, which is free from loose binding, which is not disordered, which is captivating, and where the placement of words is not too distant. (90)
His eyes have the luster of blue lotuses, his lower lip is as beautiful as the bandhūka flower, and his nose is like a golden hook;
therefore, this Victor is lovely to behold. (91)
With eyes possessing the luster of blue lotuses, lips as beautiful as the bandhūka flower, and a nose like a golden goad, this Jina is lovely to behold.
Having transcended the state of vulgarity composed of pleasant speech, one overcomes vulgarity because of the cause of [craving for] aesthetic flavor. || 92 ||
Having transcended vulgarity, the speech is refined and well-composed; because it serves as the cause for aesthetic flavor (rasa), it transcends vulgarity, which is a form of bondage. (92)
This fierce outcaste of passion torments me, now merciless and now compassionate;
why do you remain indifferent toward one who has fallen into such calamity, even though you are happy? (93)
This outcaste of lust torments me, being merciless even toward those who show compassion; why do you, though yourself happy, neglect me in such a state of calamity? 93.
The avoidance of what is deficient in ascetic practice is no longer being pursued now;
for that which causes agitation upon hearing has already been examined below. (94)
The avoidance of those who are deficient has not been further discussed here,
because the agitation caused by hearing [such views] has already been examined previously. (94)
As for one who has fallen from his desire:
"You are of noble conduct; therefore, because of that very [conduct], there is satisfaction in you.
Give me a region, or a village, or a beautiful field. (95)
An example of one who has passed away gradually is as follows:
"O you of noble conduct, because of that very [conduct], my devotion is toward you;
therefore, grant me a beautiful region, or a village, or a field. (95)
As it was said in the *Ativutta*:
"O Moon-like Lord of Sages, for the mass of rays of your glory, even this entire sky provides no space for its manifestation. (96)
An example of exaggeration (*atyukti*) is as follows:
"Even this entire sky provides no space for the expansion of the rays of the mass of fame produced by the moon-like Lord of Sages."
The speech of those with a malevolent mind is blameworthy even if it is devoid of purpose; however, for that reason, the words of the insane and others do not constitute an offense. 97.
The speech of those with a malevolent mind is devoid of purpose and irreproachable;
however, by that same principle, the speech of the insane and others is not at all blameworthy.
For example:
"The ocean is being drunk up by me,
who am today afflicted by old age."
These clouds thunder; this is Erāvaṇa, the beloved mount of Sakka. || 98 ||
For example:
"The ocean was drunk up by him; now here I am, afflicted by old age today.
These clouds roar, and Śakra’s beloved Airāvata [is here]."
One should utterly destroy that fault—the harshness of bondage—which is produced by the state of being stained by the conflict with the garland of happiness. 99.
Because it is delicate and avoids harshness, the beneficial binding— characterized by a radiant state and free from roughness— should thoroughly purify the defect.
For example:
Beholding the dissolution of form and hearing sweet voices, the virtuous, during the time of a Perfectly Awakened One, conduct themselves with their faces turned away from worldly play. (100)
Beholding the splendor of forms and hearing sweet speech, the virtuous, turning their backs on play, conduct themselves during the time of prosperity. (100)
Description of the examination of defects in the meaning of sentences— its "unripe" state is as follows: "The meditations, liberality, and virtues have been perfectly accomplished here."
There is no doubt that these are the means for attaining Nirvāṇa, enjoyments, the celestial realms, and so forth. || 101 ||
Regarding the departure [from cyclic existence], as it is said:
"The practices of meditation, generosity, and ethical discipline, when correctly accomplished, are undoubtedly the means for attaining nirvana, enjoyments, heaven, and so forth. (101)
If there is some specific distinction regarding a subject already mentioned that applies equally to those not yet mentioned, there is no fault in transposing the order [of the examples]. (102)
If a certain specific feature that was intended for a particular subject does not exist at all in those subjects where it was not intended,
there is no fault in the transgression of the sequence.
As it is said:

"Among [the categories] such as 'wholesome,' 'unwholesome,' and 'indeterminate,' the last one is indeterminate; the first two are not productive of karmic results, while the [third] is productive of karmic results. (103)
Among these—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—the last is the indeterminate;
it is the ordinary, while the first two are not ordinary. (103)
When there exists such a cause for the manifestation of qualities, there is no occurrence of a lack of propriety for those [words] that convey the actual state of affairs. (104)
When there exists such a cause for the manifestation of qualities,
there is no lack of propriety in one who describes things as they truly are.
What is known in the world as "appropriateness" (ocitya) should be understood with respect;
therein, noble persons who are preeminent poets originate from the source of instruction. 105.
That which is known in the world as *aucitya* (propriety) should be understood with great respect;
for noble men and eminent poets originate from the teaching of truth. 105.
One should avoid that which is devoid of the excellence of known propriety; then, when the nourishment of flavor has been accomplished, there may be the cultivation of what is appropriate. 106.
One who has realized the power of propriety should avoid what is devoid of propriety;
for by thus cultivating propriety, the nourishment of aesthetic flavor (rasa) is also accomplished. || 106 ||
Just as:
"May the Victor, who regarded even Māra’s approaching army as no more than a blade of grass because of his imminent victory, grant you triumph. (107)
May the Jina— who, celebrating his imminent victory, did not consider even the approaching army of Māra to be worth a blade of grass— grant you victory.
In the undertaking of arduous practices and the like, when there is no transgression or overstepping of the sequence, this conflict of broken rules finds no footing anywhere. (108)
When there is an attempt to bypass or transgress the sequence of agent, object, and so forth, this contradiction of broken structure finds no way out whatsoever. (108)
For example:
Trust in women, even those of good character, is not appropriate—just as [one should not trust] poison, a horned animal, disease, a river, or a royal family. (109)
No confidence can be placed in wicked men, in women, in poison, in horned animals, in diseases, in rivers, or in the royal court. 109.
And as it is said:
"One should always practice faith toward the Three Jewels, beginning with the pure Buddha, as well as toward the virtuous and the meritorious. (110)
When medicine has been prescribed, one should always maintain faith in the Three Jewels, beginning with the pure Buddha, as well as in virtuous and accomplished persons.
As for one who possesses passion:—
The people, their eyes longing for the pleasure of beholding the moonlight of the Lord of Sages, were filled with joy as they gazed upon him appearing on the path like the rising moon. || 111 ||
With eyes longing for the nectar of the light of the Moon among Sages, people—though they had already set out on their path—were delighted by the sight of his rays. (111)
If anything whatsoever is employed for the sake of doubt alone, such as for play and so forth, there is no fault; it is merely associated with doubt. (112)

If something is employed for the sake of mere amusement or similar purposes, even if it results in doubt, there is no fault in that which is presented as a *saṃśayasama* (the fallacy of doubt). || 112 ||
For example:
"When you have gone to your teacher's home for a second time from your own house, we shall surely attain happiness through study and other such means. (113)
When the Guru has gone from his own home to his second residence,
the student shall certainly and constantly obtain happiness through study and other such means.
"‘She is fortunate, she is his sister in the evening’—such [expressions] have been declared by all poets as not being fit for use. (114)
Expressions such as "this sister of his is fortunate" have been declared by all poets alike not to be vulgar.
The sequence of beautiful ornaments, occurring upon the removal of faulty ornaments, will be made manifest in the section on ornaments (Alaṅkāra-pariccheda). || 115 ||
When the faulty ornaments have been removed, the sequence of beautiful ornaments will come into manifestation;
thus, the chapter on ornaments shall appear. (115)
This excellent location was chosen by me alone in order to avoid crowding, by following the instructions of other teachers;
may this be understood through the great favor shown toward me by the most venerable masters.
One who desires fame should take the medicine at the proper time, even if it is bitter. || 116 ||
This excellent instruction has been composed by me following other treatises in order to avoid defects;
having learned these [defects] from the most eminent teacher through his great grace, one who desires fame should indeed thoroughly eliminate them.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Comprehension of the Avoidance of Faults," in the *Subodhālaṅkāra* composed by the great master Saṅgharakṣita.
Thus ends [the second chapter] in the *Subodhālaṅkāra* composed by the great master Saṅgharakṣita.
The second chapter, titled "Understanding the Avoidance of Faults. [Chapter Three: The Description of the Chapter on Understanding Qualities.
Venerable sir, virtues arise and faults are likewise transcended;
therefore, I shall now show those sounds by which one becomes adorned. 117.
Since virtues arise from the complete transcendence of faults,
I shall now demonstrate those words which adorn them.
Clarity, vitality, sweetness, evenness, delicacy, smoothness, loftiness, radiance, extreme distinctness, and concentration. (118)
Endowed with those qualities, the charming composition of the poet brings about for his patrons a fame that is absolutely stainless. || 119 ||
Lucidity, vigor, sweetness, evenness, delicacy,
cohesion, loftiness, beauty, clarity of meaning, and concentration.
When endowed with these qualities, the poetic composition of a wise man brings about for its authors a fame that is utterly stainless.
This series of words, charming because its connection [to the subject] is not remote and whose meaning is well-established, produces clarity as it should. (120)
Just as a sequence of words that is charming due to its connection with what is not remote, and whose meaning is well-known, generates clarity; so too [does this work].
The rays of the Sage’s lower lip, adorning his face, shine like the rays of the sun falling upon the interior of a lotus. || 121 ||
Adorning the face of the Sage,
the rays of his lower lip shine like the rays of the sun falling from the interior of a lotus.
Abundance of compounds is the lifeblood of prose;
it should be employed without confusion, just as a lover is desired by a beloved. 122.
Abundance of compounds is the very lifeblood of prose; even in verse, such [prose-like quality] is charming when it is not confused, just as that which is lovely is desired.
The Lord of Sages has a gentle smile; his white sprouts are smeared with sandalwood paste, and his single lower lip-sprout is likewise pale. 123.
The white sprouts of that Lord of Munis, anointed with the sandalwood of his gently arising smile, were surpassed by his single lower sprout, the lip.
That which has as its object a meaning denoted by words, and which arises from both concise and expanded forms, is called *pāriṇati*; it is like the transformation of milk into curds. (124)
That which, concerning the objects denoted by words, arises from both concise and expanded expression and results in maturity—that indeed is *ojas* (vigor), as for example: [Example follows]
Having kindled the True Dharma and having brought across [to safety] the world including the gods, he, together with his disciples, has passed away like an extinguished mass of fire. 125.
Having illuminated the true Dharma and delivered the world including the gods,
he, together with his disciples, has passed away like a mass of blazing fire.
May even the dust on the crown of my head attain the state of being a jewel, from which, O Victor, they rest upon the pair of your lotus feet through merit. (126)
May the bones of my head become dust,
O Jina, so that by this merit they may rest at the pair of your lotus feet.
In this regard, a constant longing for the supreme is clearly seen;
this quality arises from the application of those with sharp wisdom. (127)
In this regard, a longing for perpetual wandering is rightly shown;
this [state] arises from the application of those whose wisdom is directed toward the wandering of the Guru.
Sweetness of sound arises in two ways: through proximity to words and through the influence of euphonic combination (*anuppāsa*).
It may occur in even syllables, as in the former example, or in the transformation of phonemes (*vaṇṇāvutti*), as in the latter. || 128 ||
Sweetness consists of two types based on the proximity of words and the influence of alliteration:
the former is *samaśruti* (even sound), and the latter is the repetition of phonemes (*varṇāvṛtti*), as for example:
"When this bull among sages attained perfect enlightenment..."
From that time forth, a great festival for the Dharma arose in the world. || 129 ||
And when that bull among sages attained perfect enlightenment,
then there arose a great festival for the Dharma born in the world.
The gentle smiles of the Lord of Sages possess the splendor of a cluster of kunda flowers; laughing, they chase after the moonbeams across every quarter of the horizon. 130.
The gentle smiles of the Lord of Sages, possessing the beauty of a cluster of kunda flowers,
spread laughter as they pursue the splendor of the moon to the very ends of the quarters.
The arrangement of all very soft syllables is praiseworthy, just as this garland of jasmine flowers is adorned with a swarm of clinging bees. 131.
Alliteration is praised when composed with all soft consonants, as in this example: "This garland of *mālatī* flowers, adorned with swarms of hovering bees."
Whether with pure [colors],
or with pure [colors] mixed, or with mixed [colors], there is a threefold equality of colors, just as follows. || 132 ||
Uniformity is threefold, occurring through colors that are either exclusively soft, exclusively hard, or mixed— just as,
for example, there is uniformity consisting solely of softness.
Resembling the playful warbling of cuckoos yet possessing the grace of the speech of the Lord of Sages, it reaches the heart of the virtuous and bestows upon them peace. || 133 ||
The state of being exclusively soft and even:
the graceful discourse of the Lord of Sages, which resonates with the warbling of the cuckoo,
moves the heart and bestows bliss upon the virtuous.
Regarding the equality of those who possess only the physical form:
Who would not honor the Lord, the All-pervading One, who is worthy of honor and whose existence is to be expected? For who, longing for the means to liberation, would not revere the Lord? (134)
O Blessed One, whose equanimity is purely unyielding, who is worthy of being honored by those who are themselves worthy of honor,
you who have brought an end to existence.
Who, desiring spiritual accomplishment, would not honor the All-pervading Lord?
The mixed equality:
The Malaya breeze, made fragrant by contact with the sandalwood it has obtained, blows gently as if afraid of the wind from the suffering of the Lord of Sages. 135.
The Malaya breeze, having acquired a sweet fragrance through contact with sandalwood,
blows gently as if terrified of the wind from the mouth of the Lord of Sages.
The phonemes that are pleasant and tender, consisting mostly of soft syllables and devoid of harsh sounds, are easy to pronounce; such is the quality of "Sweetness" (Mālatā). 136.
Sukumāratā (delicacy) consists primarily of non-harsh syllables, is produced entirely from very soft sounds,
and involves consonants that are difficult to pronounce.
Passing by the dissolution of form and hearing the sweet voice, they conduct themselves well during the time of the Perfectly Awakened One, turning their backs on worldly play.
Even though devoid of ornaments, she ascends especially beautifully before the presence of the virtuous, radiant with that [inner] splendor. (138)
Even when devoid of ornaments, a woman who is radiant becomes especially beautiful when standing before virtuous people.
With horripilation like the arrangement of feathers, resounding with shouts of "Well done!", the flocks of female monkeys sported there, intoxicated by the honey of the Sage. 139.
These words of the sages, which produce horripilation like the arrangement of feathers, which are raised with the sound of shouts of "Well done!",
and which are garlands of excellent instruction, dangle here in the intoxication of joy.
Even when the meaning is extremely subtle, it pertains to the referent itself, just as in words such as "mother" and so forth, there is the praising of qualities like beauty and the like. (140)
Delicacy exists even with respect to the objects denoted by words,
as for instance in the case of words such as "dead" and the like, or the mention of things such as "remaining only as a reputation."
That which is a repository of qualities, charming through the contact of well-joined words and respected for its composition, is called *śleṣa* (punning); an example of it is as follows: || 141 ||

That which is a repository of qualities made delightful by the union of closely joined words, possessing weightiness of composition—that indeed is what is called *śleṣa* (punning or paronomastic composition), as for example: [text follows].
The splendor of the row of nails on the moon-like hand of the Buddha is indeed the very same splendor that serves as your ear-ornament upon the lotus-feet of the Lord of Sages. 142.
May that splendor of the lotus-feet of the Lord of Sages protect you— a splendor that eclipses the beauty of the crescent moon with the luster of the rows of nails that sever its illusion.
If this quality is recognized as being like a mountain stream, then by that it would be noble;
thus the path of composition becomes well-supported. (143)
Whatever quality is perceived as excellence, by that it becomes sublime; thus the path of composition is well-supported.
O Gotama, those beings whose limbs are smeared with the dust of your lotus feet—oh, they always go to a state free from dust! 144.
O Gautama, those beings whose bodies are smeared with the dust of your lotus feet— oh, they always attain freedom from all afflictions!
Thus, the power of the Victor is seen to manifest here;
one who possesses wisdom should contemplate the supreme [state] by means of this method. (145)
Thus, the excellence of the nature of the Victor is indicated here;
one who possesses wisdom should contemplate this supreme direction according to this method.
Even that which is sublime should be understood as a praiseworthy qualification, such as "the lake Koḍa," "playful laughter," or "golden bracelets," and so forth. (146)
That too should be understood as "noble" (udāra) when it possesses a specific excellence;
for example: "sporting lake," "playful smile," "golden armlet," and so forth.
It has transcended the state of being worldly and is beloved by all people; it is called "Kani" because it is spoken of as having gone beyond, and "Sā" because it is free from faults. (147)
For example: "The Lord of Sages" (*muninda*) and so forth;
such [names] do not transcend common usage and are pleasing even to all people. This is because, for one whose name is *Kānti*, there is no avoidance of the expressed sentiment (*rasa*).

Just as in the verse beginning "The Lord of Sages," the meanings, the distinctness, the designations, the flavors, the leadability, and the sounds are derived from the literal sense; this [quality] is demonstrated here as being free from both types of leadability. (148)

For example, "amarīci" (a non-ray) and so forth [are instances of] pleasing the mind, while "mārā" (the god of love) and so forth [are instances of] clarity of meaning; these consist of the suggestiveness of the word itself and the suggestiveness of the meaning.
Thus, both of these have been demonstrated in the context of the refutation of the "leadable" (neyya).
Just as in the cases of "amarīci" (83) and so forth,
and "mano'nurañjanomāra" (83) and so forth;
O steadfast one, the natural purity of your toenails is in vain.
For those infinite forests do not abandon us within the shadow of the crown-lock (mauliccha).
O steadfast one, whose nature is pure, it is in vain that you [polish] your toenails,
since the infinite worlds do not cease casting their reflections upon them.
That which the wise, acting in harmony, consider to be the essence of bondage—that quality called concentration (samādhi) has now reached the occasion for its manifestation. 150.
All learned men consider this to be the essence of bondage;
this quality named samādhi has attained the essence of the path of insight.
Having a different nature and being otherwise than that, yet conforming to the limits of the world, this which is correctly undertaken is designated as "concentration" (samādhi). || 151 ||
If other phenomena are correctly understood as being distinct from that [object], in accordance with the limits of worldly convention, it is designated as "samādhi."
The Dharma, which is itself without hands, is sometimes correctly grasped by those who possess hands;
it is formless, yet belongs to that which possesses form; and it is flavorless, yet belongs to that which possesses flavor. 152.

In the case of that which is not liquid, there is agency even for one who is not an agent; and for that which is solid, even though it is not a body, it performs the function of form for them through successive action. (153)
The nature of living beings is sometimes correctly attributed to that which is breathless;
likewise, the form of that which possesses form is attributed to the formless, the flavor of the flavorless, and the liquidity of the non-liquid;
even agency is attributed to that which is not an agent.
Even though the kaṭhina is bodiless, its form would arise from them in succession.
O Lord, I believe that even during the day, the night-lotuses, through union with you who possess a full moon of woolly hair, are free from sleep and overflowing with joy.
O Lord, those people who immerse themselves in the essence of compassion, as if in the essence of nectar, are happy and freed from faults; they are those who bow at Your lotus feet. 155.
O Lord, those people who immerse themselves in the essence of compassion as if in the essence of nectar are happy and freed from faults; they bow at Your lotus feet.
O steadfast one! Even toward sweetness there is no quality by which those who do not find favor in you might be won over;
what then can be said of the pungent qualities of their speech? (156)
O steadfast one, what kind of mental disposition is yours that you do not take pleasure even in this sweet quality? Alas, such is the nature of these bitter qualities of theirs!

Accomplishing all aims, possessing the great virtues of the Cūḷakapupphiya and Peṭaka suttas, they run in every direction with the splendor of kunda flowers and endowed with auspicious marks. || 157 ||
Accomplished in all aims, drinkable from small cups, possessing great virtues, smooth, and with the beauty of kunda flowers, they spread in every direction.
The various weapons of the enemy of Māra, once brandished, have become blunted; now, filled with shame, they bow at your feet under a different guise. 158.
O Jina! The various weapons discharged by the enemy forces of Māra became blunted and ineffective; ashamed, they fell at your feet.
The Lord of Sages, like the sun risen at dawn upon the mountain of enlightenment, shines brilliantly with the rays of the True Dharma, utterly dispelling the blinding darkness. (159)
The Lord of Sages, the sun, has risen at the time of the mountain of awakening;
he shines with the rays of the true Dharma, utterly shattering the blinding darkness.
"Vomiting and swallowing—this, being devoid of virtuous conduct, may indeed be considered very beautiful; let them know it as the vulgar way. (160)
This [ornament], such as *vamana* (ejecting) and *giraṇa* (swallowing), when not deprived of its repetition of qualities, is exceedingly beautiful; otherwise, it will certainly fall into vulgarity.
The row of rays from the sage’s toenails, under the guise of vomiting out all other beauties, as if drinking up the moonlight, renders that [moon] lusterless. 161.
Under the pretext of vomiting her own splendors, the row of the sage’s toenails makes the moon lusterless,
as if it were drinking its light.

An action performed by one who is without consciousness is merely a nominal action; however, that which is performed by one possessing consciousness is the supreme action characterized by its inherent quality. 162.
That which is produced by an unskilled artist is merely pleasing; such is the work of one possessing [only] secondary qualities.
However, that which is produced by a skilled artist is the highest form of work, characterized by excellent qualities.
Vomiting forth, as it were, the essence of affection for all people, what person would the Supreme Victor not delight by preaching the beloved Dharma?
He who is skilled in the meaning of words, proficient in dictionaries, moon-like in his mastery of ornaments, and always devoted to practice—
even if lacking in poetic composition, he may still be numbered among the poets.
Having grasped this, one finds here fame of no small measure. || 164 ||
He who is skilled in the meaning of words, proficient in the lexicon (nighaṇṭu), and has constantly applied himself to prosody and poetics—
even such a person is not counted among poets if he is devoid of the power of poetic composition.
Having immersed themselves, they attain fame of unsurpassed form.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Comprehension of Qualities," in the *Subodhālaṅkāra* composed by the great master Saṅgharakkhita.
Thus [ends] the *Subodhālaṅkāra* composed by the great master Saṅgharakkhita.
The third chapter, titled "Understanding the Qualities" (Guṇāvabodha). Chapter Four: Understanding the Ornaments of Meaning (Arthālaṃkārāvabodha).
Since those [ornaments] which are endowed with meaning and possessed of qualities are called "extremely beautiful," they shall now be discussed. (165)
Since these compositions, endowed with figures of sense (*arthālaṃkāra*) and poetic qualities (*guṇa*), are exceedingly beautiful, they shall now be described.
The ornamentation is twofold due to the division of those whose conduct is naturally crooked:
the first reveals various states of the objects [of poetry] for one's own sake. (166)
The figures of speech (alaṃkriyā) are twofold due to the distinction between those whose nature is crooked (vakravṛtti) and those that are not;
among these, the first reveals the various states of things.
O steadfast one, you who are beautiful with playful strides and whose glances survey the quarters, you shine like the splendor of the Bodhisattva; I utter these words. 167.
Charming in his playful stride, with the steady gaze of a sage,
the sprout of a Bodhisattva shone as he spoke words like those of a bull among men; for when the nature of a statement and its factual basis are otherwise, that constitutes defeat.
Its state of having infinite conceptual variations is the illustration of the seed. || 168 ||
The mode of being of a thing's intrinsic nature would be subverted if it were otherwise;
because that [nature] consists of infinite conceptual possibilities, this is merely a demonstration of its seed.

In that [chapter on figures of speech], there are: atiśayokti (hyperbole), upamā (simile), rūpaka (metaphor), āvṛtti (repetition), dīpaka (illumination), ākṣepa (paraleipsis), arthāntaranyāsa (corroboration by a general truth), vyatireka (contrast), and vibhāvanā (causation by an unusual cause). || 169 ||
The sequence of causes, the more affectionate, the compound, the metaphorical, the composed, the figurative expression, and the concealed—these are for those [types of similes]. 170.
The concealing of a specifically established ego, equal pairing (tulyayogitā), illustration for the sake of greatness, deception, and praise of what has been undertaken; 171.

The single-string necklace (ekāvalī) consists of mutual coexistence and non-opposition; it includes exchange (parivṛtti), error (bhrama), absence (abhāva), mixture (miśra), and the solitary (āsī) and paired (rasī). || 172 ||

In that regard, the poetic figures are indeed hyperbole (atiśaya), simile (upamā), metaphor (rūpaka), repetition (āvṛtti), illumination (dīpaka), paraleipsis (ākṣepa), corroboration by another matter (arthāntaranyāsa), contrast (vyatireka), and the description of the causeless (vibhāvanā).
The sequence of causes, the more beloved concise summary,
conceptualization, meditative concentration, the function of synonyms, and the description of a pretext.
Viśeṣa, Rūḍhāhaṃkṛti, Śleṣa, Tulyayogitā, Nidarśanā, and from Atiśayokti, Vakrokti (as praise not based on literal meaning), Ekāvalī, Anyonya, Sahokti, and Virodhitā.
"Revolving, wandering, existence, resting, and eating—you are [all these]."
These divisions have been fully enumerated; the state of non-existence is called life.
One who acts with crookedness nourishes [the self], but through deceit one nourishes supreme glory. (173)
These varieties have been fully described; *bhāva* (emotional state) is said to be life itself.
In crooked compositions (*vakravṛtti*), however, it is *śleṣa* (punning connection) that nourishes supreme splendor.
That which is the specific mode of operation for the excellence of the expressed meaning is called *atiśayokti* (hyperbole).
It is twofold: that which transcends the world and that which pertains to the world. || 174 ||
The excellence that constitutes the illuminator is twofold:
that which transcends the world and that which is worldly.
These divisions, beginning with birth and so forth, are both mundane and supramundane; today, however, we shall explain those whose sphere transcends the world. (175)
These Vedas set forth that which transcends the world, whereas birth and the like are merely worldly excellences.
O Lord of Jinas, those who drink the radiance of your body with the hollows of their eyes—even though you are the remover of craving—are they not capable of destroying it? (176)
O Lord of Jinas, those who drink the beauty of your body with the hollow of their sidelong glances—even you, the remover of thirst, are not able to slake their thirst; how much less can we?

The similarity between the object of comparison and the subject of comparison may constitute a simile; it is threefold: that which is understood through words, through meaning, and as pertaining to the sense of a sentence. 177.
The simile (*upamā*) consists of the similarity between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*).
It is threefold: it may be conveyed by words, by the sense, or it may have the meaning of a sentence as its domain.

Due to the influence of the words "samāsa," "paccaya," "vā," and so forth, [the compound] is threefold: that which is understood through sound by means of a compound, as in "The Lord of Sages, moon-faced. (178)

Words such as compounds (*samāsa*), suffixes (*pratyaya*), and particles (*iva*)—by virtue of these, [the meaning] is threefold. That which is understood through words by means of a compound is, for example, "the Lord of Sages, moon-faced" (*amunīndraścandrānanaḥ*).
"From those conditions such as āya and so forth, the lotus is born from their speech;
the pair of eyes of the Lord of Sages is like the petals of a blue lotus. (179)
By means of those verbal suffixes beginning with *āya*, speech is produced like a numerical calculation;
it merges into the pair of lotus-petal-like faces of the Lord of Sages.
*Iva*, *iva*, *tulya*, *samāna*, *nibha*, *sannibha*, *yathā*, *saṃkāśa*, *tulita*, *prakāśa*, and *pratirūpaka* [are synonyms for "like" or "resembling"]. (180)

The *sapakṣopamitopamā* (simile with a similar class) consists of [terms] that are similar (*sarisa*), corresponding (*sarikkhā*), concordant (*saṃvādī*), contradictory (*virodhi*), like (*sadisā*), opposing (*paṭipakkha*), or contrary (*paccanīka*). || 181 ||

Reflected image, concealed, not of the same form, equal, measured, similar in color, counterpart, resemblance, having the same nature, and so forth—these are the characteristics of a likeness. || 182 ||
He triumphs, reviles, laughs, goes back, hates; he envies, knows, censures, remembers, and obstructs. 183.
It steals away his good fortune, it robs him of his splendor;
it quarrels with him and mounts upon his very balance. 184.
He plunges into the marsh, and darkness follows after him; that is my view of his virtue which he restrains and his conduct toward it. (185)
The words beginning with *iva*— namely *iva*, *vat*, *tulya*, *samāna*, *nibha*, *sannibha*,
*yathā*, *saṃkāśa*, *tulita*, *prakāśa*, *rūpaka*, and *pratirūpaka*— [denote similarity].
Sadda, saddakṣa, saṃvādin, virodhin, and likewise saddaśa;
pratipakṣa, pratyanīka, sapakṣa, upamita, and upamā.
Reflection, image, likeness, identical form, equal measure,
same color, radiance, representative, sharing common properties, and having the same characteristics.
She triumphs, she reviles, and she indulges in laughter;
she becomes corrupt, she is envious, she despises, she censures, she is jealous, and she obstructs.
The balance robs him of his good fortune, it steals away his splendor;
it disputes with him and it mounts upon him.
It plunges into his marshland; it follows him and clings to him. They restrain him from that habit, yet he imitates him in that very way.
The similarity between the standards of comparison and the objects compared is discerned by those who possess aesthetic sensitivity;
for it is by means of these that certain varieties of simile are now being presented.
"The blooming lotus wafts fragrance; so too is the face of the Sugata beautiful.
This is called a simile of the Dharma (*dhammopamā*), which demonstrates a common characteristic. (187)
"The face of the Sugata is exceedingly beautiful, like a blossoming lotus"—
this is called a *dharmopamā* (simile based on a quality), because it demonstrates a common attribute.
"The lotus-like face of the Sage is devoid of Dharma"—this is an "Inverse Simile" (*viparītopamā*), as in: "Your face is equal to a lotus. (188)
"Devoid of dharma, yet resembling the lotus-face of the Sage"—this is the *viparītopamā* (inverse simile). "Your face is equal to the moon"—this is the *tulyopamā* (simile of equality).
"Your face is like a lotus, and a lotus is like your face"—this is mutual simile (aññamaññopamā), because there is a mutual comparison. 189.
"Your face is like a lotus, and a lotus is like your face"—
this is mutual comparison (*anyonyopamā*), because each serves as a standard of comparison for the other.
"If there were some lotus possessing the grace of your eyes and eyebrows, so that it might bear the beauty of your face"—this is a marvelous simile. (160)
"If there were some lotus possessing the playful charm of a wandering glance,
and it could bear the splendor of her face— then that would be a marvelous simile."
"Is it your face, endowed with the excellence of fragrance and beauty, that rivals the moon's rays, or is it a lotus? This is considered *śleṣopamā* (simile based on paronomasia). 161.
"Your face, possessing the excellence of fragrance and beauty, and rivaling the rays of the moon, is like a lotus"— this is indeed considered a *śleṣopamā* (metaphor based on paronomasia).
The simile of continuity expressed by words of identical form is as follows:
"She is beautiful like a grove of *sāla* trees in a garden frequented by children. (162)

When expressed by words of identical form, that is the simile of the continuum (*santānopamā*), as in: "This is a young woman, beautiful with her forest of hair, like a grove of *sāla* trees adorned with a garland of young sprouts."
"The moon in the sky [is surpassed] by the lotus with its many pollen-dusts; though equal to them, your face excels them"—this is considered a "censure simile" (nindopamā). 163.
"The moon is subject to waning and the lotus is full of dust; yet your face is equal to them both and even surpasses them"—this is considered a "defective simile" (nindopamā).
"O Moon, you are unable to roar back at the Conqueror with your mouth;
you are but a mere ornament for the water. This would be a simile of prohibition. || 164 ||
"O Victor, the moon is incapable of roaring in response to you;
it is dull and stained"—such would be a *pratiṣedhopamā* (prohibitive simile).
"Having surpassed the beauty of the filaments of the white lotuses, your face is like itself"—this is an incomparable simile (asādhāraṇopamā), because [the object] is produced as its own equal. (165)
"Having surpassed the region between the moon and the sun, your face has become equal only to itself"— this is an *asādhāraṇopamā* (an incomparable simile).
"Your face shines as if it were a mass of the essence of all ambrosia gathered together somewhere"—this is a simile based on what has become a reality (bhūtopamā). 166.
"Your face shines as if it were some mass of the very essence of the luster of all lotuses gathered together in one place"— this is an "unprecedented simile" (abhūtopamā).
However, in some instances, a compound, a suffix, and so forth, is understood from the inherent power of the word, even without the explicit connection of a word. 167.
However, in some cases, it is understood through the power of the words as being implied by the sense;
this occurs even without the use of compound words or suffixes.

"These eyes are like blue lotuses, and this face is indeed a lotus"—when such a comparison is made through a clearly established similarity, it is considered a simile based on identity (*sārūpyopamā*). (168)
These bees are indeed [bees], not a lotus; that is merely a face.
Because the similarity of meaning is clearly manifest, this is considered a simile based on identity (*sārūpyopamā*).

"Enough with this boasting of the moon, 'May it indeed possess the radiance of my face,' since that [radiance] exists even in a lotus; this is therefore a *parikalpopamā* (a metaphor based on an assumption). 169.
Enough with this boasting of the moon that "the beauty of her face resides in me alone," for one must consider it a mere delusion that such beauty exists even in a lotus.
"Is it a bee hovering over a lotus? Or is it a face with tremulous eyes?
My mind wavers"—this is the simile of doubt (*saṃśayopamā*). (200)
"Is it a bee wandering within a lotus, or is it a face with tremulous eyes?
My mind wavers thus"—this is the simile of doubt (saṃśayopamā).

Furthermore, because it demonstrates a certain basis and expresses a similar property, the *upamā* (simile) arises from the cognition of similarity; for example, "as the comparison of the moon to the face. (201)

*Prativastūpamā* (the simile based on a corresponding object) occurs when, by mentioning a property that is common [to two things] after first pointing out some particular object, a perception of similarity becomes possible; for example—
When the Jinas are born, there is not even one who is their equal;
indeed, there is no second tree like the Pārijāta.
Among beings as they are born, there is no one equal to a Jina;
indeed, there is no second tree like the Pārijāta.

If any meaning of a sentence is compared to another sentence-meaning itself, that simile of sentence-meaning (vākyārthopamā) is of two kinds, according to whether it is joined with or separated from the particle *iva*. (203)
If one sentence-meaning is compared to another sentence-meaning, that simile of sentence-meanings (*vākyārthopamā*) is of two kinds: either joined with the particle *iva* or separated from it.
This Victor has appeared among people for those scorched by the defilements, like a rain-cloud in the season of Dharma for those tormented by the heat of the teachings. (204)
This Victor has appeared for the sake of people tormented by afflictions,
like a cloud at the proper time for those scorched by the heat of the lack of Dharma.
The face of the Lord of Sages shines, uniquely captivating in its grace;
even that which has risen high above is uniquely captivating in its grace.
O Moon! What further expansion do you display?
That which causes confusion for the wise by means of a different gender and so forth is capable of being a flaw in a simile; this is illustrated as follows: || 206 ||
That which causes confusion for the wise by having different genders and so forth is sufficient for the purpose of refuting a simile;
this has been explained as follows:
"This moon is like a swan," where the genders are different.
Those of a different caste are low; a servant is one who has undergone consecration for his master. || 207 ||
"This moon is like a female elephant" is an example of different genders (*bhinnaliṅga*);
"like arrows from a bow" is an example of words denoting different classes (*vijātivacana*).
A soldier who has eaten his meal yesterday [is fit for duty] when the lord is present.
"The firefly shines like the garlanded sun" is an *adhikopamā* (hyperbolic simile).
"The ocean, its depths unbreached, was agitated like the elephant-headed one [Ganesha]" [is an example of a simile where the object of comparison is not explicitly stated]. (208)

"He shines like a garland of glowworms" is an instance of an excessive simile (*adhikopamā*). "The moon, though possessing a spot, is a treasury of white lotuses" is an instance of a fragmentary simile (*khaṇḍitopamā*). (209)

"The moon's spot is like a bee"—this [example] depends upon a simile (*upamā*). An example of the *khaṇḍitā* [type of heroine] is: "The night-maker (the moon) has the form of a white lotus and is possessed of a spot."
In such forms as these, they become devoid of respect;
however, the wise show respect only toward certain specific applications.
Thus, the wise become indifferent toward such forms as *ityeva* and the like,
yet they show regard for them only in specific applications.
“This person goes like a woman, yet they say, ‘This one is like a man’;
this [other] person is like my life-breaths, while knowledge is like wealth acquired. (212)
"This person goes with a woman," "She speaks like Umā," "This one is as dear to me as my own life."
"Acquired like the wealth of knowledge."
"O Protector of the Earth! The King of the Gods shines like you;
he is not able to rival you in splendor."
The non-perception of the difference between the object of comparison and the subject of comparison, wherein the distinction has become obscured, is called *rūpaka* (metaphor). 213.
The object is either the whole (asesavatthu) or a partial aspect (ekadesavivatti);
each of these two is further divided into three types: by way of the aggregate (samāsa), the day (divasa), and so forth. || 214 ||
Because of the determination of the non-difference between the standard of comparison and the object compared,
*rūpaka* (metaphor) is held to be nothing other than *upamā* (simile) with its distinction obscured.
It has for its object all things without exception, as well as those that manifest only in part;
furthermore, this [poetic suggestion] is again threefold by virtue of compounds and other such elements.
Who indeed would not wear upon their heads the lotus-feet of the Lord of Munis, which possess filaments of the brilliance of nails beautified by the luster of their rays?
Abounding with the jewels of virtues, possessing the cool water of compassion, and characterized by profundity and unfathomability—this Victor is a manifest ocean. 216.
Abundant jewels are his virtues, and compassion is his cool water;
this Jina is visibly a deep and unfathomable ocean.
O Lord of Sages, this gentle smile from the moon of your face well awakens the forest of white water-lilies that is my mind. (217)
This moonlight of gentle smiles from the moon-like face of the Lord of Sages awakens the forest of white water-lilies that is the minds of the virtuous.

This is the classification of metaphorical figures (*rūpaka*) regarding objects that are complete in their parts; now, the classification concerning partial concealment (*ekadesavivatti*) is being stated. (218)
This distinction regarding the subject matter of all things indeed exists in *rūpaka*;
however, I shall now describe the various types found among those that are "partially manifest" (*ekadeśavivartin*).
"Who indeed does not find happiness when beholding the face of the Sage, which has the flower of playful laughter and the tender sprout of a radiant lower lip? (219)
O Sage, those who behold her face— whose flower is a playful smile and whose tender sprout is a radiant lower lip— do not find happiness even in heaven.
May the pair of feet of the Lord of Sages grant you victory;
may his beautiful nails, with their supreme rays, conquer all evil.
May the pair of feet of the Lord of Sages grant you victory—
those feet whose toenail-rays are exceedingly beautiful, like banners of victory over sin.
Upon the moon-like face of the Lord of Sages, whose cheeks are perfectly stainless,
the forest of night-lotuses consisting of the hearts of the virtuous has fully blossomed.

There are indeed many figurative expressions (rūpaka), distinguished by various combinations; they are not mentioned separately here, as their limit is reached within these very [categories]. || 222 ||
Thus, although there are many figurative expressions (rūpaka) distinguished by what is appropriate or inappropriate,
they have not been explained separately here, as they are all included within these very [categories].
Whose mind, O steadfast one, would not be drawn by your captivating face, which is like a pool of white lotuses with its flickering eyes as bees? (223)
The phrase "the moon [shines] upon the lotus" is a fragmentary simile (khaṇḍarūpaka); it is defective, whereas "the eyes are a forest of blue lotuses," and so forth, is beautiful. 224.
