O steady-minded one! Whose mind, indeed, would this captivating face of yours—not a mere lotus, but with white flowers for its water and flickering eyes for its bees—not entice?
The moon is seen as a sky-lotus; this is a *khaṇḍarūpaka*.
"The eyes are a forest of lotuses," and so forth, is beautiful.
There is no limit to conceptual constructions regarding form and its similes; therefore, this [Nirvana] is to be understood as unsurpassed through inference. 225.
However, there is no limit here to the varieties of metaphors involving physical forms;
therefore, it should be understood that what has not been explicitly stated is to be inferred.
The repetition of both a word that has already been uttered and one that follows it is to be understood by the name *āvutti*. (226)
The repeated utterance of a meaning, of a word,
or of both— this is to be known by the name *āvṛtti* (repetition).
It captivates the minds of all, it takes up the ten directions, and it seizes stainlessness; this is the mass of glory belonging to the Conqueror. 227.
It captivates the minds of all, it draws [glory] from the ten directions,
and it grasps the stainlessness of the Victor’s fame.
The radiance of the Sage’s body illuminates all directions, shining forth as if it had eclipsed the light of the moon and other celestial bodies.
The splendors of the Sage’s body illuminate all directions;
they outshine even the moon and other luminaries as if they were eclipsed.
Having conquered the enemy of the afflictions in this world, this Victor dwells [in peace];
yet this host of enemies dwells among the wicked like a heap of living beings.
Having conquered the enemy of the afflictions in this world, this Victor dwells [in peace];
yet this host of enemies dwells as if gathered into a heap within the wicked.
Even when occurring in only one place, that which assists the entire sentence is called "the illuminator" (dīpaka); it likewise has as its scope the beginning, the middle, and the end. (230)
For that which exists in one place is indeed beneficial to the entire sentence;
it is called *dīpaka* (the illuminator), and it is threefold, pertaining to the beginning, the middle, or the end.
The Buddha brought about the immeasurable prosperity of his kinsmen who were to be trained, and he simultaneously crushed all evil and the various non-Buddhist sects. (231)
The sight of the Sage is considered a blessing by virtuous people;
for other beings, however, it is a poison that causes constant torment.
Whose heart would not be captivated by the moon-like face of the Jina, which is as enchanting as the moonlight of the most lovely beauty? (233)
Whom would the moon-like face of the Jina—not to mention the [ordinary] moon—not delight? It possesses the most extreme beauty of loveliness and is as enchanting as moonlight.
Virtue is the cause of freedom from remorse; it is the cause of gladness; that [gladness] is the cause of rapture; and this [rapture] is the cause of tranquility for the sake of accomplishment. 234.
Virtuous conduct free from regret is the cause of joy;
that [joy] is the cause of delight, and this [delight] is for the sake of achieving renown and so forth.

Thus, even in the case of *dīpaka* (illumination), a series of sentences proceeds such that each preceding one depends upon the one following; this is considered *mālādīpaka* (garland-illumination). || 235 ||
Even when functioning as an illuminator (*dīpaka*), if a series of sentences proceeds such that each subsequent one depends upon each preceding one,
that is considered "the lamp of a series" (*mālādīpaka*).
In this very manner, those of pure intellect should discern the underlying principles of the remaining types of illustrations as well. (226)
In this very manner, those of pure intellect should establish the sequence of the remaining alternatives in the *Aidīpaka*.
But that which is a statement of negation when there is a desire for a specific statement is called "objection" (ākṣepa); and it is threefold according to the distinction of time. (237)
When there is a desire to state a specific distinction, that which is a statement of negation is called *ākṣepa* (paralipsis); and this is threefold according to the division of time.
How did that victorious Jina, alone, conquer that Māra with his vast army? Or rather, how great was the power of his perfections (pāramī)? || 238 ||
Alone, that Victor defeated Māra, who possessed many armies;
how else could it be, for such is his supreme power?
Why do you despair, thinking, "I have not yet attained the complete eradication"?
Is it not the case that even a single prostration made toward the Sugata is itself such an eradication? 226.
"Why do you feel dejected, thinking, 'I am devoid of even a little merit to be extracted'? For has not even a single prostration been offered in this way to the Sugata?"
Those wicked people whose minds are overwhelmed by wrong views will not go to that truth which is auspicious and all-enchanting. (240)
It is true that those wicked people, whose minds are enveloped by false views, will not go to the auspicious state that is the domain of the virtuous.

That which establishes the meaning of another sentence by means of a placement within [its own] meaning is the "all-pervading" (sabbavyāpi) type; for it is distinguished as "specific" (visiṭṭha) according to its particularity.
Even those who stand for the welfare of the world—the sun and the moon themselves—will go to their setting; who can transgress the fixed law? (242)
Even all those who act for the welfare of the world, including both the sun and the moon, will depart, abandoning their purpose; by whom can this natural law be transgressed?
The Teacher of gods and men, that Lord of Sages, has likewise attained Nibbāna; for all conditioned phenomena are indeed impermanent. 243.
The Teacher of gods and humans, that Lord of Sages who has mastery over himself—he too has passed into final peace; for all conditioned phenomena have ceased, and the Teacher no longer remains.
The Victor leads people from the wilderness of saṃsāra to Nibbāna; is this not indeed a fitting course for one who possesses self-confidence? (244)
The Victor leads people from the wilderness of saṃsāra to nirvāṇa;
indeed, is it not fitting that this is the destination of one who possesses the fearlessnesses?
O Victor, your lower lip, being so flavorful, delights the mind;
those who are themselves overcome by passion delight others when they associate with them. (245)
O Jina, your lower lip is so flavorful that it delights the mind;
for those who are themselves overcome by passion surely delight their companion.

Furthermore, based on whether the subject is expressed or implied, and based on the similarity of the entities, this contrast (vyatireka) is fourfold, distinguished by the divisions of "one," "both," and "neither. (246)
When the expressed meaning is to be understood through the similarity of objects, there is a classification [of simile].
This negative concomitance (vyatireka) is also of one kind, yet it is fourfold due to the distinction between both [the probans and the probandum].
O Jina, you are equal to Janadhina in qualities such as profundity and greatness; the difference between you, however, lies in this body of yours.
O Victor, you are equal to the ocean by virtue of qualities such as profundity and greatness;
the only difference between you and it is this body of yours.
The Great Being is profound like the ocean, and the Sugata is likewise;
the Jina is like the ocean in color, resembling añjana, yet possessing the radiance of gold.
The Great Being and the Sugata are both exceedingly profound, like the ocean;
the Victor resembles the color of the sea, while the Conqueror has the luster of gold.
O Lord of Sages, your pair of deer-like eyes does not merely dispel distress nor grant only desired objects; it is adorned with those very virtues. 246.
O Lord of Sages, neither do I find the heat of passion nor the granting of desired objects in those deer-eyed women; rather, it is your pair of eyes, adorned with such virtues, that captivates me.
The lotus of the Lord of Sages is unlike this [ordinary] lotus; while this [lotus] bestows well-spoken words that convey the Truth, the face is not such a lotus. 250.
The lotus-face of the Lord of Munis is like this for them;
it bestows the nectar of excellent conduct, whereas such a lotus-mouth does not exist elsewhere.
Where, having set aside a manifest cause, another cause is presented, or where the intrinsic nature [of a thing] is made manifest, that is "suggestion" (vibhāvanā). 251.
When a well-known cause is set aside by positing another cause,
or when a thing is conceived as being due to its own inherent nature, that is *vibhāvanā*.
Your eye is not curved nor dark, your lower lip is stained a rosy-red;
O Jina, your face is even in luster, high in stature, and free from crookedness. 252.
O Jina, your eye is not cast askance nor is it dark; your lower lip is stained a lovely crimson; this gait of yours is even and without wandering, and you are never devious.
Indeed, even a wicked person does not cry out when meeting with another wicked person;
for the minds of virtuous beings are exceedingly pure by nature. (253)
Indeed, even wickedness does not cry out when meeting with the wicked;
yet it does so in the minds of virtuous people, which are exceedingly pure by nature.
Causes are of two kinds: the producer and the informer; their function as ornaments has been explained in the Paṭisambhidāmagga. (254)
Due to the influence of existence and non-existence, and also due to the influence of the cause of consciousness, their divisions are infinite; this is merely a brief indication of them. || 255 ||
The causes of a thing are of two kinds: those that produce it and those that make it known;
however, their refinement is declared to be the nature of poetic figures (alaṃkāra).
Due to the influence of existence and non-existence, as well as the influence of forms and causes, there are infinite distinctions; this, however, is merely a brief illustration of them.
O Lord of Munis, this teaching of yours—whose essence is the illumination of the ultimate truth and which is enchanting to all—truly delights my mind. (256)
O Lord of Munis, these teachings of yours, which have the singular flavor of illuminating the ultimate truth and captivate the minds of all, fully satisfy my heart.
Through dwelling with the wise, through application to the true Dharma, and through the restraint of the sense faculties, there may be the pacification of suffering. || 257 ||
Through dwelling with the steadfast, through application to the true Dharma,
and through the restraint of the senses, there shall be the pacification of suffering.
O Moon-like Lord of Sages, you who shine with a lovely nature that accords with the moon.
As if making it clear with his own mouth, he declared that his mind was free from evil. || 258 ||
O Moon among the Lords of Sages, by your very face, which shines with a lovely luster that accords with yours,
it is clearly understood that your mind has emerged free from evil.
O Lord of Sages, how is it that the tender morning sunlight of passion touching the pair of your lotus-feet causes your lotus-hands to close? 256
How is it that your lotus-like hands clearly cause the tender morning sunlight of the red hue of the pair of feet of the Lord of Sages to contract?
The rays of the moon-like nails of the Lord of Sages cause the lotuses of the faces of living beings to close. 260.
The rays of the moon-like nails of the two feet of the Lord of Sages cause the lotus-buds of the hands of living beings to close here.
The enumeration of the meanings of the terms already mentioned is given in their respective order;
"according to number" (yathāsaṃkhya) is defined as both the correspondence of numbers and the sequence of order.
O Lord of Sages, through your playful conversation and smiles,
the cuckoos and the night-lotuses alike attend upon you in the forest and by the water.
O Lord of Sages, because of your victory, the cuckoos and the night-lotuses attend upon the forest and the water with their playful chatter and laughter.
There may indeed be something dearer than any material wealth; namely, that which consists in the bestowing of what is dear upon one who is dear. (263)
It may indeed be that for some person, the form of an object is more dear;
yet the communication of that [object] would occur only through an excess of affection for it.
The joy that has arisen within me because of your peaceful teaching will become joy for you as well when we meet again in due time. (264)
The joy that has arisen within me from the sight of you, O Holy One,
shall in time become even greater through seeing you once again.

This [type of simile] is called the "compound expression" (samāsavutti), because it expresses the intended object through a descriptive comparison by way of a conventional designation of meaning. (265)

This is called *samāsokti* (abbreviated expression), which consists of the nature of a semantic convention (*arthasaṃketa*), wherein the intended object is [conveyed] by means of a description through a metaphorical function (*vṛtti*).
In the evening, by one who is intoxicated with distinction, there exists another [cognition] characterized by non-distinct and distinct qualifiers;
indeed, there is yet another characterized by both distinct and non-distinct qualifiers. (266)
In the evening, [the cognition] is qualified by the mere substantive as having both distinct and non-distinct qualifiers;
likewise, there exists another [cognition] which also has both distinct and non-distinct qualifiers.
Bestowing pure minds upon those who approach, this ocean of enlightenment is deep and possesses a treasury of radiant jewels; yet it has not been attained by me through merit alone. (267)
For this ocean, a treasury of jewels, is praised as being pure, vast, and deep; and it has been brought forth by me through my own heat.
This essence that grants desired goals, adorned with flowers and fruit, has arisen like a marvelous wish-fulfilling tree (kapparukkha) endowed with beautiful shade. 268.
Bestowing desired objects, the essence of all things, and adorned with fruits and flowers,
this tree has arisen like an unprecedented Kalpa-tree, providing excellent shade.
The Jina was praised by Sāgara with the *ṭeṭha* sound, while Rukkhatta praised him with the *indita* sound;
all these are common qualities [of praise], except for that which occurs previously or otherwise. (269)
The True Dharma is proclaimed as the ocean, and the Victor as the tree;
all qualities are common to both, yet in the former case there are three [qualities] not found elsewhere.
When the occurrence of a thing in a different mode than it actually exists is conceptualized, that is "conceptualization" (parikappanā). (270)
When the existence of a thing is conceived in a manner other than its actual state, that is "otherness" (tadanyatā);
where such [a conception] occurs, it would be a false conceptualization (parikalpanā).
Based on the internal meaning of comparison and by way of action and so forth, I shall provide various examples of imaginative construction according to their respective functions. (271)
I shall describe in sequence various conceptualizations based on internal meaning through comparison and by the power of action and so forth. She sat,
distressed by the frustration of her desire, motionless and full of envy.
He dwells as if entering that steadfast state through the application of yoga. || 272 ||
Then those celestial nymphs sat motionless, distressed by the frustration of their desires,
as if they were bringing that steadfast man under their control through the application of their amorous arts.
Māra, mounted upon his elephant, is rushing forward for battle;
he seeks the path, but there is no escape for one who has been conquered by you. (273)
Māra has mounted an exceedingly tall elephant for battle;
indeed, O Jina, he is seeking a path to flee out of fear.
I imagine that the crimson hue of the lotus-like feet of the Lord of Sages, which are as beautiful as lovely rājīva-lotuses, arises from the blood produced by the crushing of his own sins. 274.
I consider the beautiful pair of lotuses at the feet of the Lord of Munis to have acquired their crimson hue from the blood produced by the crushing of my sins.
By means of such words as "I think," "I suspect," "surely," and "as if," suggestion (*vyañjanā*) is manifested in some cases, while in others it is understood through the sentence as a whole. (275)
By means of words such as *manye*, *śaṅke*, *dhruvam*, *nūnam*, and *iva*,
this [suggestion] is manifested in some cases, while in others it is understood through the sentence as a whole.
O Victor, those whose bodies emit rays of light moist with the flow of compassion nourish virtuous people; it is not fitting for them to possess a lack of essence.
O Jina, those whose beauty has emerged from their bodies, being full of compassion and restraint, delight the virtuous; is this not their very essence?

When one who is undertaking whatever task it may be gains, through the power of merit, the acquisition of the necessary means for its accomplishment, they call that "concentration" (samāhita). || 277 ||
But whatever little one may do out of delight by the power of merit,
such that there is the attainment of other means of accomplishment— that they call "concentrated" (samāhita).
For that Teacher, whose mind was intent on the destruction of the enemy Māra, the great earth, the great sky, and the sun were all helpful. 278.

The wise ones say that because he saw his desired goal as being otherwise than through success, that [statement] was spoken figuratively. 276.
Although his desired [result] has been shown to be otherwise through its accomplishment,
those of pure intellect call that [accomplishment] a figurative application (paryāyavṛtti).
This wealth is laid open in the courtyard, free from any need for guarding;
O seeker of wealth, go as you please and take whatever you desire. (280)
O seeker of wealth! This treasure has been deposited in a secluded courtyard and is free from guards;
go as you wish, if you so desire.
One who praises while appearing as if censuring that [person] does so by means of deceptive qualities;
for here indeed, faults appear as virtues and come into close proximity. (281)
In this [poetic figure], even while praising, one speaks as if censuring; for under the guise of such description, apparent faults turn out to be virtues that come into close proximity.
O Kuvalayākhila, you are indeed capable of shaking [the world] violently;
yet, O Lord, we declare that even by that much, there is no distinction among your virtues. (282)
O Lord! You are fully capable of shaking the entire world of blue water-lilies;
what need is there for us to speak further of your extraordinary virtues?
When there is a deficiency in the substance, action, genus, or quality intended for specification, that [deficiency] is what is called "specification" (visesa).
Where there is the observation of a deficiency in the substance, or in its action, genus, or quality, due to a desire for excellence, that is what is called "distinction" (viśeṣa).
There were no chariots, nor elephants, nor horses, nor foot-soldiers;
indeed, the enemy Māra was conquered by the Sage through the power of mindfulness alone. 284.
There were no chariots, nor elephants, nor horses, nor foot soldiers;
for the enemy Māra was conquered by the Sage through the accumulation of the requisites.
The Sage, the steadfast and supreme one, did not knit his brows nor did he quiver his lip; yet he himself made known the defeat of the enemy Māra. 285.
Neither did the Buddhas, nor even their lower lips, quiver;
the Sage himself, the best of the steadfast, brought about the destruction of the enemy Māra.
The sun does not shine in all directions, nor does the world illuminate the world;
nevertheless, the well-spoken word of the virtuous dispels the darkness that lies beyond.
The light of the sun does not pervade all directions, nor has its radiance spread throughout the world;
nevertheless, a well-spoken word is a supreme dispeller of the blinding darkness.
O Lord of Sages, your words are neither harsh nor indeed [harsh];
nevertheless, they thoroughly uproot the intoxication of the people.
O Lord of Munis, your words are neither harsh nor arrogant;
nevertheless, they dig deeply and uproot the pride of the people.
The wise declare that such speech as "rūlhāhaka" and the like is used when a monk displays his heroic valor by saying, "But the leftovers are being given. (288)
If one displays an exceedingly radiant heroism and valor,
the wise describe such a state as being rooted in verbal pride.
“O lady, what need have I for seeing Nanda and Upananda? My sons, who are devoted to serving my feet, are ready whenever such [a task] arises. (289)
"Give [it] to Nanda and Upananda; what use have I for seeing your activities? My sons, devoted at my feet, are indeed ready for such a task."
śleṣa (punning) is defined as that which consists of multiple meanings expressed by a single word;
it is said to be threefold based on its occurrence in non-distinct words, sentences, and so forth. (290)
śleṣa (paronomasia) is that [figure] wherein a single word possesses multiple denotations;
it is said to be threefold on account of its occurrence within a non-differentiated word, a sentence, and so forth.
Having ascended to the great exaltation that removes the blinding darkness, this Blessed One, garlanded with rays of light, shines as he awakens the people. 291.
Dispelling the blinding darkness, captivating, and having ascended to great exaltation,
this Blessed One, garlanded with rays, shines forth, awakening all people.
Resembling the *sāradā* and *āmalaka* fruits, with its exhaustion brought to an end, the awakening that has the form of a white water-lily nourishes the people of pure intellect. (292)
Shining with the luster of an autumnal *āmalaka* fruit, having brought about the exhaustion of all afflictions,
and possessing an awakening as beautiful as a white water-lily, the wise one brings joy to the people.
The Sugata, the Leader, whose mind is concentrated, who has subdued pride and intoxication, and who is stainless—may he protect all living beings. 293.
May the Sugata, the Guide, who possesses the discipline of meditative concentration, who crushes pride without exception, protect all living beings with clarity.
The other [type of negation] is that which possesses a restricted scope, whose action is both distinct from and non-distinct from what is opposed and non-opposed;
it expresses both the restriction and its exclusion, and is thus both non-contradictory and contradictory. || 264 ||
"The phrase 'the nourisher and so forth' is a type of compound (padajāti) formed by eliding [the middle term].
Its specific form will become evident through these very examples. || 295 ||
The supreme [agent] possesses actions that are both contradictory and non-contradictory, yet remains undivided;
he is possessed of discipline, expresses discipline through implication, and is both non-contradictory and contradictory.
"Appropriateness, sentiment, and so forth, as well as *śleṣa* (paronomasia), belong to the word (*pada*) and the genus (*jāti*).
The nature of these will become manifest in their very illustrations.
When there is strife in even a small portion of this entire world, the enemy of Māra is defeated and the King of Dharma manifests his power. (296)
May this entire world be protected in every way by him whose body is composed of the arts;
the enemy of Māra is being defeated, and the King of Dharma is flourishing.
People hear the words of the Sage, which are sweet by nature and arise from the emergence of extraordinary merit, and they behold the Deathless.
People hear the speech of the Sage, which is naturally sweet, meritorious, and born of a special excellence; they behold it as nectar.
With his speech and his demeanor, the Jina dispels the darkness and delights the minds of living beings with his natural sweetness. (298)
Just as the Victor strikes away darkness with his speech and radiance, which are sweet by their very nature, so too does he gladden the minds of living beings.
The blackness of the hair, the curvature of the eyebrows, and the ruddiness of the hands, feet, and lips belong only to the Lord of Sages. (299)
The blackness belongs only to his hair and eyes, and the curvature only to his eyebrows; while the palms of his hands, the soles of his feet, and his lips possess a deep red hue, O Lord of Sages.
Your passion is seen only in your hands, feet, and lips; yet, O Lord, that very same passion is also seen in this assembly of virtuous ones. 300.
This passion of yours is seen only in hands, feet, and lips;
or rather, O Lord, it is seen even in the virtues of the virtuous.
Possessing his own distinctive marks, exceedingly fortunate, radiant, and destined for rising, the Lord of the World, who has conquered all afflictions, shines forth as the sovereign of ascetics.
Gentle, exceedingly handsome, radiant, and of certain rising,
that Lord of Jewels shines forth in the world as the Master of Men who has conquered all afflictions.
Though peerless, he is not peerless in the world; though the lord of the world, he is unsurpassed. Though compassionate, he is also without attachment—even this is the range of the Sage’s mind. 302.
Though peerless, he appears equal; though the Lord of the World, he is unsurpassed; though compassionate, he is merciless toward evil—wondrous indeed is the way of the Sage!
The people of the world, bowed down and afflicted by the suffering of saṃsāra, find the deathless nectar you bestow—the ultimate happiness they desire. (303)
The people of the world, afflicted by the suffering of saṃsāra and bowed down,
find in you that which grants desired happiness and even ultimate immortality.
When there is a mention of something after having made it equal to other things possessing similar qualities, that is considered the figure of speech known as Tulyayogitā (Equal Pairing). 304.
When something is described by placing it together with other objects possessing similar qualities, that is considered *tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing).
The world possesses worldly prosperity, and the Blessed One possesses the prosperity of the world;
for both are suns that dispel darkness.
Both have attained the light of prosperity and have attained the wealth of illumination; for both are garlanded with rays and are Blessed Ones who dispel darkness.
When establishing another matter, that which is shown as a similar result—whether it be non-existent or existent—is an illustration (nidassana). || 306 ||
If, while establishing an internal [logical connection], one shows some result that is similar—
whether it be existent or non-existent— that is called "illustration" (nirdaśanā).
Through the rising of the Lord of Ascetics, evildoers go to ruin; for those who oppose the King of Dharma, even their good conduct reaches a miserable end. 307.
Upon the rising of the Lord of Śramaṇas, evils go to their defeat;
for the conduct of those opposed to the momentum of Dharma ends in ruin.
With his foot placed upon the head, the Jina demonstrates to the world his own supreme wonder, which is like that of a marvelous lotus. 308.
Placing his feet upon the heads [of his disciples], this Jina, who removes the waters of existence, makes known his own supreme wonderfulness in the world.

Whether it be for the sake of greatness through sovereign power or for the sake of one's own intention, that which has reached the highest excellence is declared to be "for the sake of greatness. (309)
That which, by its manifestation, possesses a great object, or by its pervasiveness, has attained supreme excellence— that is declared to be the "great object" (mahad-artha).
In former times, the Bodhisatta, whose sunshade was interlaced with the radiance of the jewels on his diadem, went forth after having been worshipped by supreme glory.
In former times, the Bodhisattva, adorned with supreme beauty and holding a sunshade interlaced with the radiance of jewels from his crown, went forth.
That Bodhisattva, intent on perfect enlightenment for the sake of the welfare of beings, abandoned even his mother, Rāhula’s mother, though she was bound to him by the bonds of affection. 311.
The Bodhisattva, possessed of the nature of awakening, for the sake of the welfare of beings,
abandoned even his mother Rāhula’s mother, though she was bound to him by the essence of affection.
If, having concealed the restriction of its color, anything else is shown instead—whether it be dissimilar or similar—that is considered deception. (312)
If, having concealed the restriction of color, anything else whatsoever is shown—
whether dissimilar or similar— to that [object], it is considered deception.
Neither among thousands nor among five [thousand] was there anyone like the Tathāgata;
Māra saw that among others there was this thousand increased tenfold. (313)
Neither among thousands nor among five thousand was there anyone like him;
even Māra, who rules over others, possesses ten times a thousand [of such followers].
"Engaged in dispute with the moon that is the face of the Lord of Sages, this full moon has not abandoned the power of the Mind-born [God of Love]. (314)
Engaged in debate with the moon-like face of the Lord of Munis, [the opponent] thought:
"This is not the full moon; it is merely the crescent of the Mind-born God."
The praise that arises here from following others and so forth is a praise of the small; this is what is called "praise of the small. (315)
When praise is offered for something that has not been mentioned by describing something else,
that praise regarding the unmentioned subject is called Aprakṛtastuti (Praise of the Unrelated).
The deer live happily in the forests, serving no one else, on water, grass, sprouts, and the like, which are obtained without effort. (316)
The deer live happily in the forests, subsisting on wild roots; for they obtain water, darbha grass shoots, and other such things without any exertion.
Where each subsequent term serves as a qualification for each preceding one, that is the "Single Strand" (ekāvalī); it is of two kinds, by way of affirmation and negation. (317)
Where each subsequent term serves as a qualification for each preceding one, that is Ekāvalī; it is of two kinds, according to affirmation and negation.
The rows of the Teacher’s toenails, beautiful with their rows of nails, radiant with rays of light, and whose rays possess the singular flavor of destroying darkness, shine forth. (318)
The feet of the Teacher shine with rows of nails that are radiant with rays; those rays, whose sole purpose is the dispelling of darkness, are resplendent.
For an ascetic, contentment is not destroyed by lack of contentment, nor is it destroyed by stinginess;
yet for living beings, stinginess brings about endless calamities. (319)
A mendicant who is not content is indeed destroyed by his longing for satisfaction;
he is like a net that brings endless calamity to living beings.

When the state of being adorned belongs to two objects that are mutually distinct, yet they possess a mutual similarity even without [external] adornment, that is the ornament of mutual adornment (aññamañña-vibhūsana). || 320 ||
When two things, which are ornaments of the earth,
are such that one is seen as an ornament for the other in order to negate their mutual difference, that is indeed "Mutual Ornament" (anyonyam bhūṣaṇam).
By that Sage, the Kinsman of the World, a circle of light a fathom wide was emitted;
he too thereby attained a great and corresponding radiance.
By that Sage, the friend of the world, the great orb of radiance was attained;
he too has acquired such splendor through him.
The statement of coexistence, of action, and of quality should be understood as "co-occurrence" (sahavutti); here are examples thereof. || 321 ||
The mention of coexistence, action, and quality is to be understood as "co-occurrence" (sahavṛtti); an example of this is as follows.
The rays from the Teacher’s fingernails shine like the crest of the moon’s beams,
and the moonlight of his face glows equally with the moon.
The rays of light from the Teacher’s nails shine together with the moonbeams,
and your moon-like face blossoms along with the moon.
Sin becomes defiled along with the mind of the wicked at the rising of the Victor; the quarters become perfectly pure along with the mind of the virtuous. 324.
Sin, together with the mind of the wicked, is darkened by the rising of the sun;
the quarters of the sky, together with the mind of the virtuous, are perfectly pure.
Where there is a display of association between two contradictory meanings, that is considered "contrariety" (virodhitā) for the purpose of expressing excellence. (325)
Where there is an observation of the association of contradictory things for the purpose of expressing excellence, this is considered the figure of speech known as Virodhitā (Apparent Contradiction).
Even virtues, though sweet by their very nature, when cultivated by one who associates with the wicked, truly defile the mind of that friend of the world. (326)
Even virtues that are sweet by their very nature, when cultivated toward the sole friend of the world, corrupt the minds of those who serve evil.
The taking up of any particular gift or any particular object by someone [else] is considered to be "exchange. (327)
The giving of anything whatsoever in exchange for the taking of something else that is superior is considered *parivṛtti* (exchange).
In the past, the Sage did not grant others the favor of his gaze and so forth; now, however, he has attained the glory of knowing the fitness [of recipients]. 328.
Having previously given away his charming eyes and other organs to others,
the Sage has now attained the glory of omniscience.
When one acts with a slight lack of clear understanding, that is "equal" (sama);
it is considered a state of delusion regarding a matter from which doubt has not yet departed. (329)

Having seen something, however, the cognizer may act upon it as if it were that [other thing]; when an object is thus apprehended while its doubt has not yet been removed, this is considered "error" (bhrama).
Beholding the rays from the nails of the Victor’s feet shining equally in all directions, people whose minds are like the moon rejoice. (330)
Beholding the moonlight-like radiance of the Jina’s toenails shining equally upon the radiant quarters, people whose minds are free from passion rejoice.
That by which the state of being of things is made known is called "name" (nāma) and so forth; by whatever attribute a state of being is designated, that is termed a "name. (331)
If it is said that the awakening of emotion (bhāva) for poets occurs through names and so forth, this emotion is declared to be expressed by any letter whatsoever.
Are not those very oceans, which do not overstep their boundaries even when agitated, your lineage?
For they do not abandon their limits even when filled to the brim.
Are not those very ones—the oceans, the mongooses, and the mountains—their lineage?
For even in their minds, they do not transgress their boundaries, even when rained upon.
Furthermore, when there is a relationship of mutual subservience (*aṅgāṅgībhāva*) or a state of having similar effects (*sadṛśaphalabhāva*) among figures of speech,
that conjunction of ornaments is called "Mixture" (*miśra*).
The great river of the rays from the foot-nails of the praised sage—oh, how it brings only joy to those people who are deeply immersed in it! 334.
Behold, sirs! This great river of light from the rays of the Sage’s toenails,
though it plunges people deeply beneath it, brings them nothing but happiness.
The Sage’s appearance is sweet by its very nature, his form is an elixir for the eyes, and his speech is like honey; it does not fail to delight the people. 335.
His attire is naturally sweet, his form is an elixir for the eyes;
like honey, O Sage, in whom does his speech not bring delight?
Just as the word "āsī" (he was) signifies the beginning of a matter, may the Lord, the sole refuge in the three worlds, protect the world that approaches him. 336.
If my desired purpose were to be fulfilled,
may the Lord, the sole refuge of the three worlds, protect the world from calamity.
That ornament which produces the perception of aesthetic flavor (rasa) should be known as "possessing flavor" (rasavanta) by way of its method of possessing flavor. || 337 ||
That which, by means of its ornaments, gives rise to the perception of rasa (aesthetic flavor) is to be known as *rasavat* (possessing rasa),
according to the rule for the presence of rasa.
The feet of the Teacher of the Three Worlds, possessing an extraordinary passion for the necks of lotus-like faces bowed in devotion,
have taken up a firm and constant embrace with their hands that are ever moist with affection.
They kiss him thus with an agitation born of their affection for his welfare. || 338 ||

Taking firmly with his ever-fresh trunk the two feet of the Lord of the Three Worlds— whose face is a wondrous lotus blooming from the ocean of passion, and who is adorned with the hue of the Bandhūka flower— [the elephant]...
For they indeed gather together with such haste for the sake of what is beneficial.
Thus, following the power of the former conduct,
this classification of the *Yamalaka* verses— which have been elaborated upon by successive poets— has been succinctly declared.
Who indeed would be able to behold them all around? || 339 ||
Having observed the rules previously composed [by others],
that which constitutes the various categories of divisions and subdivisions of the ornaments has been stated here in brief; enough with further elaboration.
Who indeed would be able to describe it all?
Thus ends the chapter titled "The Comprehension of the Ornament of Meaning" in the *Subodhālaṅkāra* composed by the great master Saṅgharakkhita.
The Fourth Chapter. Thus ends the "Understanding of Figurative Meanings" (*arthālaṃkārāvabodha*) in the *Subodhālaṃkāra* composed by the great master Saṃgharakṣita.
The Fourth Chapter: The Chapter on the Comprehension of Rasas and Bhāvas,
[composed] by one possessed of eloquence who follows worldly convention.
It was composed by a poet who thoroughly understood the arousal of the various emotional states (rasas). || 340 ||
The stable, the suggestive, and the excitants, together with their consequents, become the causes for the attainment of the essence of rasa by those who are virtuous. (341)
Then, by a poet who possesses inspired eloquence, who follows worldly conventions, and who understands how to bring forth aesthetic propriety, [the work is produced] to the highest degree.
The stable emotions (sthāyibhāvas), along with their determinants (vibhāvas) and consequents (anubhāvas),
when properly composed and presented, lead to the aesthetic relish (rasāsvāda) of the virtuous.
Since specific modifications of mental activity bring forth the aesthetic flavors (rasas), therefore love and the other emotions are designated by the term "bhāva" (emotional state). || 343 ||
The specific modifications of the mental state (cittavṛtti) bring forth the aesthetic flavors (rasas);
therefore, love and the other emotions are designated by the term "bhāvas" (transitory states).
This entity, which is not concealed by the existence of its opposite, stands firm through its own nature;
thus it is designated as a "static entity" (aṭṭhāyībhāva). || 343 ||
That state which is not obscured by a contrary or other state,
and which persists by its own nature, is designated by the term "permanent emotion" (sthāyibhāva).
Delight, laughter, sorrow, anger, envy, fear, loathing, wonder, and equanimity—these nine abide in the mind. (344)
Delight, mirth, and sorrow, anger, energy, and likewise fear,
disgust, wonder, and tranquility— these are the nine stable emotions (sthāyibhāvas).
Those who practice with a discipline characterized by such distinctions as concealment and manifestation become inconsistent in their conduct. || 345 ||
Those who, through their conduct, practice concealment and manifestation and so forth in a non-primary manner, become characterized by deviation.
The faculties of penetration, equanimity, self-confidence, and serenity; dullness, dejection, and restlessness; sleep, laughter, illness, anxiety, joy, mindfulness, and impudence.
Anxiety, pride, negligence, intoxication, madness, delusion, awakening, the onset of sleep, shame, death, fickleness, and disease—these are the [twenty-one] secondary afflictions. 346.
Despair, reasoning, doubt, fatigue, fortitude, dullness, dejection, ferocity,
lassitude, sleep, laughter, languor, longing, joy, recollection, envy, despondency, and dissimulation.
Anxiety, pride, epilepsy, indignation, memory, madness, delusion, awakening, sleep,
impetuosity, shame, death, fickleness, and disease— these thirty-three are the transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāvas).
Because your mind is concentrated, beings are brought to non-existence by you; even your weapons, through your power, become non-substantial for them. (347)
Sattva arises from the state of meditative concentration;
by that [sattva], those sattvic secondary emotions (anubhāvas) are produced, and they become distinct states for you.
Stiffness, perspiration, horripilation, as well as sweating, trembling, change of color, and tears—these are indeed the seven involuntary physical states (sattvikabhāvas). || 348 ||
Stupefaction, fainting, horripilation, as well as perspiration, tears, trembling, change of color, and loss of voice— these eight are indeed the sattvika emotions.
When emotions such as love and the like are not established upon the foundation of steadfastness, then all those emotions become transitory. || 349 ||
When states such as love (rati) and the like do not possess the quality of stability,
then all those states become transitory (vyabhicārin).
The *vibhāva* is the cause among them, as well as the excitant (*uddīpana*);
that which serves to awaken them is called the *anubhāva*. (350)
The *vibhāva* is the cause for their [the emotions'] arising and their intensification;
that which serves as their awakener is called the *anubhāva*.
Having discerned the various causes, the specific activities of the mind, the underlying disposition, and the manifestations of power, Viṇṇiya sent a letter of greeting.
In order to clearly distinguish the specific mental activity arising from various causes,
one should explicitly describe the state [of emotion] through its determinants (vibhāvas) and consequents (anubhāvas) within the poetic composition.

Those various emotional states (bhāvas), together with their determinants (vibhāvas) and consequents (anubhāvas), should be described according to their respective fitness, in accordance with worldly conventions. 352.
Those very determinants (vibhāva) and consequents (anubhāva),
as well as the transitory states (vyabhicāribhāva), should be described according to their fitness and propriety by one who follows the conventions of the world.
Due to the excellence of her mental activity, she was free from sweat; externally, she appeared as if adorned by her majestic powers. (353)
Because they are specific modifications of the mental consciousness and are composed of the *sattva* constituent,
one should describe them as external manifestations such as perspiration and so forth, which are the *anubhāvas* (consequent effects).
The joy of the audience that follows the meaning of the bond—because they relish it, those who know it call this "rasa. (354)
That bliss which belongs to the audience who follow the meaning of the composition is called *rasana* (tasting) by the experts; therefore, it is designated as *rasa* (aesthetic flavor).
When that very rasa is brought to a state of being relished through the vibhāvas, the anubhāvas, the sāttvika bhāvas, and the vyabhicāribhāvas, it remains as the stable essence itself. || 355 ||

Indeed, it is the stable emotion (sthāyibhāva) itself, when brought to a state of relish through the determinants (vibhāvas), the consequents (anubhāvas), the involuntary states (sāttvikas), and the transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāvas), that constitutes aesthetic flavor (rasa).
The erotic, the humorous, the pathetic, the furious, the heroic, the terrifying, the loathsome, the marvelous, and the peaceful are the nine aesthetic flavors (rasas) in their successive order. 356.

The aesthetic flavors (rasas), following the sequence of their stable emotions (sthāyibhāvas), are: the erotic, the comic, the pathetic, the furious, the heroic, the terrible, the loathsome, the marvelous, and the peaceful.
This Ānanda is of the nature of suffering; how indeed could there be compassion and the like for him?
For Ānanda would have been the sorrow of Vessantara. 357.
How indeed could there be joy in that which is of the nature of suffering, such as compassion and the like?
For while there is joy for the listeners, there is sorrow for Vessantara.
The enjoyment of delightful places, times, seasons, and attire, and the mutual passion and delight of the young, is called *rati* (pleasure). || 358 ||
The delight experienced by young people who are mutually enamored, arising from the enjoyment of beautiful places, arts, seasons, dress, and so forth, is called *rati*.
Through their power and influence, those bonds nourish him;
they act in three ways according to the state of association, dissociation, or enjoyment. (356)
Those mental states (bhāvas) and their consequent manifestations (anubhāvas), when bound together by means of logical reasoning, nourish that [rasa];
and that [rasa] is likewise threefold, according to the influence of separation through non-union, separation through union, and enjoyment.

Through the movement of transformation and so forth, whether in oneself or another, there is laughter; through sleep, lassitude, intoxication, and other such transitory states, one laughs even more when nourished by them, as does the female sex and others. (360)
For laughter arises from deformities, strange arrivals, and so forth— whether directed toward oneself or another— accompanied by transitory emotions such as sleep, weariness, and fainting.
Upon its full development, that [laughter] becomes predominantly directed toward women and the like.
In this world, one perceives among the twice-born (brahmins) a smile with wide-open eyes that is white;
a laugh with a sweet sound; and a derisive laugh accompanied by an uneven trembling of the body. || 361 ||
That which is struck by water is called *apahamita*; that whose limbs are scattered is *vikkhitaṅga*; and that which is excessively struck is *atihamita*.
Two and two *hasta*s are stated for these respectively in the order of the eldest, the middle, and the youngest.
Here, a smile with blossoming eyes,
and upon perceiving some bird, a laugh with blossoming eyes.
A smile with a sweet voice is [the first]; a laugh accompanied by shaking the shoulders and head is [the second].

The *apahasita* (slight smile) is characterized by moist eyes; the *atihasita* (excessive laughter) involves the tossing of the limbs. These two types of laughter are said to occur respectively among the superior, the middling, and the inferior [beings]. Furthermore, there are the *sokarūpa*, *karuṇa*, *niṭṭhappa*, and *tiṭṭharāsana*.
In that regard, the transitory states (vyabhicāribhāvas) are weeping, fleeing, paralysis, and so forth;
as well as despondency, indolence, death, anxiety, and the like. (363)
Karuna (the pathetic sentiment) consists of sorrow arising from the occurrence of the undesired or the loss of the desired;
its transitory states (anubhāvas) include weeping, fainting, paralysis, and so forth,
while its transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāvas) include despondency, lassitude, death, anxiety, and the like.
The rasa known as the Oppressive (rūdha) arises from anger, stinginess, and so forth; from pride and the like; and from the eyes, the dawn, and so on. (364)
The rasa named Raudra (the Furious) arises through anger, insults, and the like; through nourishment, fear, intoxication, and the like; and through redness of the eyes and so forth.
In this world, effort characterized by majesty and prowess is designated as "heroic.
Due to its application in battle, giving, and compassion, this heroism is of three kinds. (365)
Dejection, mental distress, and so forth are transitory emotional states (vyabhicāribhāvas) arising from the power of fate. || 366 ||

Energy (utsāha), characterized by majesty, valor, and so forth, is designated as "heroism" (vīra). Due to its association with battle, generosity, and compassion, this heroism is of three kinds. These same states—fortitude, intelligence, and so on—are the transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāvas).

The *vikāra* (alteration) here consists of trembling and so forth; the *anubhāva* (consequent effect) consists of perspiration and so forth; and the *vyabhicāribhāva* (transitory emotion) here is terror and the like. (367)
The *bhayānaka* (the terrible) consists of an intensification of fear through such things as deformed postures and curses;
its *anubhāvas* (consequent effects) here are perspiration and the like, and its *vyabhicāribhāvas* (transitory mental states) are terror and so forth.
Through detachment from the foul, such as urine and so forth, it is loathsome;
through agitation and trembling, it is gradually accompanied by compassion. (368)
The nourishment of this [aesthetic experience] does not arise from fear and the like through such things as snakes;
rather, this wonder regarding the meaning of words that transcend the world is what constitutes the marvel of rasa. (369)

The *bībhatsa* (the loathsome) arises from disgust toward blood and the like, or toward putrid things and the like, through the process of detachment. It is joined with compassion by means of agitation and distress;
its nourishment comes from the contraction of the nose and so forth, as well as from fear and the like.

Indeed, this wonder arising from rasa, produced by objects that transcend the world, has its attendant expressions (anubhāvas) such as exclamations of "Well done! and the like; and in this case, terror, agitation, fortitude, and wisdom are the transitory mental states (vyabhicāribhāvas). (370)
Its manifestations (anubhāvas) may be perspiration, tears, expressions of praise, and so forth;
the transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāvas) are fear, agitation, fortitude, and discernment. The dominant emotion (sthāyibhāva) arises from compassion, joy, and the like.
But for those who are truly peaceful, the states of existence and so forth are difficult to endure, having been thoroughly renounced. || 371 ||

The stable emotion (sthāyibhāva) arises from love, friendliness, compassion, joy, and the like; its excellence is brought about by [the other] emotions and so forth, and this Quiescent Rasa (śānta) is cultivated by the virtuous.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Comprehension of Rasas and Bhāvas," in the *Subodhālaṅkāra* composed by the Great Master Saṅgharakkhita.
Thus [ends the work] by the son of the illustrious Ravinātha Avasthita, who was devoted to the supreme Brahman and honored among the eminent scholars.
The *Subodhālaṅkāra*, composed by the great master Saṃgharakṣita, as translated by Avasthī, who bears the title of *Ḍākṭara* and Brahmamitra.
